questions.wrong: Both produce the exact same query result — a child row with no matching parent. The difference is entirely causal, not structural: an orphan's FK was already broken the moment the row was created (bad import, bypassed validation). A dangling reference was perfectly valid when created, and only became broken because the parent row was deleted afterward. You need an archive/audit log to tell which one you're looking at.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say cascade deletes (ON DELETE CASCADE) are 'not always the answer' for a deleted customer's orders?
choices: Many business scenarios need to retain orders for audit, revenue reporting, or legal compliance even after the customer is deleted — soft-deleting the customer instead keeps the FK relationship intact
ON DELETE CASCADE is not supported in SQL Server
Cascade deletes always run slower than manual deletes
Cascading would delete the Customers table itself
questions.right: Right — automatically deleting the orders along with the customer would erase exactly the records finance and audit need to keep. Soft-deleting the customer (IsActive = 0) preserves the history while still marking the relationship as no longer active.
questions.wrong: The instinct might be "customer deleted, so cascade-delete their orders too" — but orders often need to survive for revenue reporting, audits, and legal retention requirements, independent of whether the customer record itself still exists. The lesson's suggested fix is to soft-delete the customer instead of physically removing the row, which keeps the FK relationship intact rather than creating a dangling reference at all.

questions.q: What does summing up the stranded revenue attached to dangling-reference orders actually accomplish, beyond just counting the broken rows?
choices: It converts a data-quality flag into a business metric finance can act on — a specific pound/dollar amount that's currently unattributable, not just an abstract row count
It automatically fixes the dangling references
It deletes the affected orders
It has no practical value beyond the row count
questions.right: Exactly — "47 broken rows" is an engineering fact. "£847.50 of revenue can't be attributed to a customer for reporting" is something finance actually has to act on. Same underlying query, very different audience.
questions.wrong: A row count tells an engineer something is broken. A revenue figure tells finance something they need to fix — money that currently can't be correctly attributed to any customer in reporting. Grouping by the deleted CustomerID and summing TotalAmount turns a technical data-quality issue into a number a non-technical stakeholder can prioritize against other work.

G03-T02.close: You've now got the vocabulary to tell two identical-looking SQL results apart by their actual cause — which matters because the fix for each is different. Self-Referencing FK Violation is next: what happens when a table's foreign key points back into itself.

G03-T03.open: New shape entirely: a table whose foreign key points back at its own rows — an org chart, where an employee's manager is just another employee. Let's see how that can break in ways a normal parent-child FK never could.

questions.q: Why does the lesson insist on running the self-loop and circular-reference checks BEFORE using the recursive CTE to walk the org hierarchy?
choices: A recursive CTE that hits a circular reference will loop indefinitely until SQL Server throws a MAXRECURSION error — checking for loops first prevents building a query around data that will crash it
Recursive CTEs are always slower than the validation checks
SQL Server requires all self-referencing tables to be validated before any query can run
The checks and the recursive CTE test completely unrelated things
questions.right: Exactly — a circular chain gives a recursive CTE nothing to terminate on. It'll keep walking A → B → A → B forever until the recursion cap stops it with an error. Fixing the loops first means the hierarchy walk actually has a chance of succeeding.
questions.wrong: Think about what a recursive CTE actually does: it keeps following the chain until it runs out of new rows to follow. If A reports to B and B reports to A, there's no natural stopping point — the CTE will keep looping until SQL Server's MAXRECURSION limit kills it with an error. Running the self-loop and circular checks first means you catch and fix the loop before you try to build a report on top of broken data.

questions.q: Check 3 joins the Employees table to itself with `A.ManagerID = B.EmployeeID AND B.ManagerID = A.EmployeeID`. What does this specific pattern detect?
choices: A two-way circular loop — A manages B, and B also manages A, at the same time
Every employee who has ever changed departments
Employees who report to themselves directly
The total headcount of the company
questions.right: Right — both conditions have to be true at once: A's manager is B, AND B's manager is A. That mutual pointing-at-each-other is exactly what a two-person circular loop looks like in a self-referencing table.
questions.wrong: Read both halves of the join condition together: A.ManagerID = B.EmployeeID means A reports to B. B.ManagerID = A.EmployeeID means B ALSO reports to A. Both being true at the same time is a genuine contradiction — two people each claiming to manage the other — which is exactly the two-way circular loop this check is built to surface.

questions.q: What is the ReportingPath string (e.g. `E010 > E001 > E003`) built by the recursive CTE actually useful for?
choices: If an employee's own ID appears twice in their path, that reveals a circular reference in the hierarchy they're part of
It's purely cosmetic formatting with no diagnostic value
It calculates each employee's salary based on hierarchy depth
It replaces the need for the ManagerID column entirely
questions.right: Exactly — the path is a visible trail of everywhere the walk has already been. If a node shows up twice in its own path, the walk has looped back on itself, which is unambiguous proof of a cycle.
questions.wrong: The path string records every node visited on the way to the current one. If you ever see the same EmployeeID appear twice inside its own ReportingPath, that's direct evidence the walk looped back to somewhere it had already been — a circular reference. The lesson also notes unusually long paths (more than ~10 levels) as a secondary signal of likely data entry errors.

G03-T03.close: Self-referencing tables add a whole new failure category that normal parent-child FKs don't have — loops. Circular Reference in Hierarchy is next, going beyond simple two-way loops into chains of any length that eventually curve back on themselves.

G03-T04.open: Last lesson caught direct self-loops and two-way loops. This one goes further: what about a loop that takes five, ten, or twenty hops to get back to where it started?

questions.q: How does building a VisitedPath string as the recursive CTE walks the hierarchy help detect a circular reference of any length, not just two hops?
choices: If the next node the walk is about to visit already appears somewhere in the accumulated path, the walk has looped back on itself, regardless of how many hops that took
The path string is only used for display purposes and has no detection role
It counts the total number of employees in the company
It only works for loops of exactly three nodes
questions.right: Exactly — the path doesn't care how long the loop is. Whether it takes 2 hops or 15, the moment the walk is about to revisit a node already in its own trail, that's proof of a cycle, at any depth.
questions.wrong: The path accumulates every node the walk has passed through so far. The check `VisitedPath NOT LIKE '%node%'` — testing whether the next node to visit is already somewhere in that trail — works regardless of how long the chain is. A 3-hop loop and a 15-hop loop are both caught the same way: the walk is about to step onto ground it's already covered.

questions.q: The lesson offers a second, simpler detection method: flag any employee 'not reachable from a root.' Why does this work for cycles of any depth?
choices: A node inside a circular chain can never be reached by walking downward from a true root (a node with no manager), because the chain never actually connects back to a root — it only connects to itself
Every employee is always reachable from a root by definition
This method only detects self-loops, not longer chains
It requires manually listing every employee in the company first
questions.right: Right — a cycle is, by definition, disconnected from the real hierarchy. It might reference real employee IDs, but the chain of managers only ever points back into the loop, never out to a genuine root. Walking down from every real root and flagging who was never visited catches exactly that.
questions.wrong: Think about what a circular chain actually is: a set of nodes that only point to each other, never to a real root (someone with ManagerID IS NULL). If you walk the tree starting from every genuine root and mark everyone you reach, anyone left unmarked was never connected to a real root at all — which is exactly what being trapped in a cycle means, no matter how many hops the cycle has.

questions.q: The lesson calls MAXRECURSION 'both a safety cap and the reason Checks 1–3 in G03-T03 must be run first.' What does this connect back to?
choices: Without fixing simple self-loops and two-way loops first, a recursive CTE walking the hierarchy will hit a circular chain and either loop until MAXRECURSION throws an error, or silently stop short of the real answer
MAXRECURSION has nothing to do with the earlier lesson
G03-T03's checks are only relevant to Credit Risk, not Data Validation
MAXRECURSION automatically fixes any circular references it finds
questions.right: Exactly — this is the payoff of doing the simpler checks first. Clean up the obvious loops (self-loops, two-way loops) before attempting any deep recursive walk, or the walk itself becomes the thing that breaks.
questions.wrong: This directly ties back to the previous lesson: G03-T03's Checks 1–3 catch the simplest loop shapes (self-loops, two-way loops) before you ever try a full recursive hierarchy walk. Skip that step, and the recursive CTE here will run straight into whatever loop exists and either error out at the recursion cap or produce an incomplete, misleading result.

G03-T04.close: You've now got detection for loops at every depth — direct, two-way, and multi-hop — plus a simpler shortcut that sidesteps needing to track paths at all. Many-to-Many Junction Table Violation is next: what happens when a table exists purely to connect two other tables, and one side of that connection breaks.

G03-T05.open: Junction tables don't have data of their own — their whole job is connecting two other tables. So what does "broken" even mean for a table that's just a bridge?

questions.q: Why must a junction table's FK be validated on BOTH sides, not just one?
choices: The relationship depends entirely on both foreign keys being valid — checking only one side leaves the other side's violations completely invisible
SQL Server automatically validates one side and requires manual checks only for the other
Junction tables never have more than one foreign key
Checking both sides is only necessary for tables with more than 1000 rows
questions.right: Exactly — a junction row's whole purpose is representing a connection between two specific parent rows. If either side is broken, the connection itself is meaningless, so both sides genuinely need their own check.
questions.wrong: A junction table exists purely to represent a relationship between two other tables — its rows have no independent meaning. If you only check that SalespersonID is valid and never check the other side, a broken relationship on that unchecked side goes completely undetected. The lesson is explicit: always validate both directions, not just the more obvious one.

questions.q: The lesson checks that Quarter is one of 1, 2, 3, or 4 — but its own Explanation says this ISN'T actually a referential integrity check. What kind of check is it instead, and why does it appear in the same query anyway?
choices: It's a domain/range integrity check, not a FK check — but it's combined here because a junction row can have a perfectly valid FK and still be semantically meaningless if its other values are invalid
It actually is a FK check, and the lesson's explanation is simply wrong
Quarter is checked against a real ForeignKey to a Quarters table
It's a performance optimization with no validation purpose
questions.right: Right — the lesson is careful to name this distinction itself: a valid SalespersonID plus an invalid Quarter is a junction row that's referentially fine but still garbage. Combining both kinds of checks in one query reflects that a junction table's real health depends on more than just its foreign keys.
questions.wrong: The lesson states this directly: the Quarter check is domain integrity (is this value within a valid range), not referential integrity (does this value point to a real parent row). They're combined in the same query because a junction table's real-world validity depends on both — a row can have a perfectly valid SalespersonID and still be meaningless if Quarter is 5, which doesn't exist.

questions.q: What does the composite uniqueness check (GROUP BY SalespersonID, Year, Quarter HAVING COUNT(*) > 1) catch that the FK checks alone would miss?
choices: A salesperson somehow having more than one sales target row for the same quarter — a data entry error or reload bug, not a broken relationship
Salespeople who don't exist in the Employees table
Quarters that fall outside the valid range of 1-4
It duplicates exactly what the FK checks already find
questions.right: Exactly — this is a different failure mode entirely. Both FKs can be perfectly valid, Quarter can be a legitimate value, and you can still have the same salesperson accidentally given two targets for the same quarter, which the FK checks would never catch.
questions.wrong: This check is looking for something the FK validity checks can't see at all: duplication. Both FKs being valid and Quarter being a legal value says nothing about whether a salesperson accidentally got two separate target rows for the exact same quarter — which typically signals a reload bug or a data entry mistake, the same duplicate-detection pattern from the Uniqueness group, applied here to a junction table specifically.

G03-T05.close: Junction tables need three different kinds of validation working together — both FK directions, domain checks on the non-key columns, and uniqueness on the combination. Cross-Database FK Violation is next: what happens when the parent table isn't even in the same database.

G03-T06.open: Every check so far has stayed inside one database, where SQL Server can at least theoretically enforce the relationship. This lesson steps outside that boundary entirely.

questions.q: Why can't SQL Server enforce a foreign key constraint that points from a table in one database to a table in a different database?
choices: FK constraints in SQL Server are limited to tables within the same database — there's no `FOREIGN KEY REFERENCES OtherDatabase.dbo.Table` syntax, even on the same server instance
Cross-database FKs work fine, this is a myth
It's a licensing restriction that can be removed by upgrading SQL Server
It only affects databases on different physical servers
questions.right: Right — this is a hard structural limit, not a configuration setting. Even two databases sitting on the exact same server instance can't have a FK constraint declared between them.
questions.wrong: This isn't a setting you can turn on — SQL Server's FK constraint syntax simply has no way to reference a table in a different database, full stop, even when both databases live on the same physical server. That's exactly why the lesson calls this "entirely the responsibility of the application layer and validation scripts" — nothing in the schema itself can catch it.

questions.q: What's the actual advantage of the 'snapshot into a temp table' pattern over querying the remote database live for every row?
choices: The cross-database round trip happens once to populate the temp table, then all the local validation runs at local speed — instead of one remote round trip per row being checked
Temp tables are permanent and never need to be recreated
It bypasses the need for any validation at all
It only works when the remote database is offline
questions.right: Exactly — one remote trip instead of thousands. Pulling the reference data over once and then validating locally is dramatically cheaper than reaching across the database boundary for every single row.
questions.wrong: A live cross-DB query run inside a NOT EXISTS for every row means one remote round-trip per row being checked — slow, and it blocks entirely if the remote system is unreachable. Snapshotting the remote IDs into a local temp table means exactly one round trip total, after which every row of local validation runs at normal local speed against data already in hand.

questions.q: Since SQL Server cannot enforce this relationship at all, where does the lesson say the responsibility for cross-database integrity actually lives?
choices: Entirely in application code, scheduled validation scripts, and documentation like a data dictionary listing every cross-database dependency and its validation schedule
It doesn't need to live anywhere — the relationship is unimportant
In a special SQL Server cross-database constraint mode
Solely in the judgment of whoever writes the application code, with no documentation needed
questions.right: Exactly — with no schema-level enforcement possible, the only thing standing between this relationship and silent drift is deliberate process: validation scripts that actually run, and documentation that says they should exist in the first place.
questions.wrong: Since the database itself can't be relied on to catch this, the lesson is explicit that responsibility shifts entirely to people and process: application-layer validation, scheduled reconciliation checks that alert on non-zero counts, and a documented data dictionary that explicitly lists every cross-database reference so nobody forgets it needs checking.

G03-T06.close: Cross-database relationships are the sharpest example in this group of a rule that matters but that the database genuinely cannot enforce for you. Soft-Delete FK Violation is next — a case where the FK IS inside one database, is perfectly valid, and is still functionally broken.

G03-T07.open: Here's a case where the foreign key constraint does everything it's supposed to, and the data is still wrong. Let's see how a valid FK can still point at a functionally dead parent.

questions.q: Why does a proper FK constraint fail to catch an order referencing a soft-deleted (IsActive = 0) product?
choices: An FK constraint only checks that the referenced row exists — it has no concept of an IsActive flag, so a soft-deleted row still satisfies the constraint perfectly
FK constraints check IsActive automatically in SQL Server by default
Soft-deleted rows are physically removed from the table, so this scenario is impossible
The FK constraint would throw an error in this exact case
questions.right: Exactly — 'does this row exist' and 'is this row still meaningful' are two completely different questions. The FK constraint only ever answers the first one.
questions.wrong: The FK constraint's entire job is checking whether the referenced row physically exists in the parent table — and P009 does exist, it's just flagged IsActive = 0. Whether that flag makes the reference functionally dead is a business rule the schema knows nothing about. Only an application check or a validation query like this one can catch it.

questions.q: Why does this check use a plain INNER JOIN to Products instead of a LEFT JOIN?
choices: The FK is already known to be valid — the row exists — so the query isn't looking for missing parents (which needs LEFT JOIN), it's looking for parents that exist but are inactive (which INNER JOIN handles directly)
INNER JOIN is required whenever filtering on a boolean column
LEFT JOIN cannot be combined with a WHERE clause
It's purely a stylistic choice with no functional reason
questions.right: Right — this is a deliberate, meaningful choice, not a style preference. LEFT JOIN is the tool for "does a match exist at all"; INNER JOIN plus a filter is the right tool once you already know it does and you're filtering on that match's attributes.
questions.wrong: Earlier lessons in this group use LEFT JOIN specifically to find rows with NO match at all. This lesson is different — the product genuinely exists, so there's nothing missing to find. INNER JOIN correctly assumes the match exists and lets the query filter on that matched row's IsActive value directly, which is both simpler and more intentional than a LEFT JOIN would be here.

questions.q: Why does the query specifically exclude orders with Status IN ('Cancelled', 'Returned') from the flagged results?
choices: A cancelled or returned order referencing an inactive product isn't actually a problem — that order was already resolved, so there's nothing left to fulfil against the now-inactive product
Cancelled and Returned orders never have a ProductID value
SQL Server automatically excludes these statuses from all JOINs
It's an arbitrary filter with no business reasoning behind it
questions.right: Exactly — the check is specifically hunting for orders that would still try to fulfil against a dead product. An order that's already closed out has nothing left to break.
questions.wrong: The whole point of this check is finding orders that WILL try to fulfil against a product that no longer exists in active inventory. A cancelled or returned order is already closed — there's no future fulfilment attempt to worry about, so flagging it would just be noise. The exclusion keeps the results focused on orders that are still open and would actually hit the problem.

G03-T07.close: You've now seen a case where the schema-level constraint is completely satisfied and the data is still broken from a business standpoint — a reminder that "exists" and "valid" aren't the same question. Cascade Delete Orphan Check is next: verifying that a delete which was SUPPOSED to clean up everything actually did.

G03-T08.open: A cascade delete ran, no errors were thrown, the ticket got closed. This lesson asks the question nobody asked at the time: did it actually work all the way down?

questions.q: Why doesn't `ON DELETE CASCADE` on Customer→Orders automatically also cascade Orders→Transactions?
choices: Cascade behavior must be explicitly configured on every FK in the hierarchy that should cascade — it does not automatically chain to the next level down unless that FK also has ON DELETE CASCADE set
SQL Server always cascades through every level of a hierarchy automatically
Cascading is limited to exactly one level by a hard SQL Server limit that cannot be changed
Transactions can never be deleted by any cascade rule
questions.right: Exactly — each FK's cascade behavior is its own independent setting. Configuring it at one level tells you nothing about what happens at the next level down, which is precisely how the OrderItems table in the scenario got left behind.
questions.wrong: Each foreign key's ON DELETE behavior is configured independently. Setting CASCADE on the Customer→Orders relationship says nothing about what happens on the Orders→Transactions relationship — that FK needs its own CASCADE setting, or deletes stop there. A multi-level hierarchy needs cascade explicitly configured at every single level for a delete to fully propagate.

questions.q: What is the pre-deletion scope check (Step 4) actually for, run BEFORE the DELETE happens?
choices: It shows exactly how many rows at each level will be affected, preventing accidental large-scale deletions and documenting the expected scope for an audit trail
It permanently deletes the rows it counts
It's a performance test unrelated to the actual deletion
It only works after the deletion has already happened
questions.right: Right — this is a look-before-you-leap check. Seeing "3 orders, 7 transactions" before running the delete means no surprises about scope, and gives you something concrete to point to afterward if anyone asks what was supposed to happen.
questions.wrong: This runs before anything is deleted, specifically to answer "what am I actually about to affect?" Seeing the exact row counts at each level ahead of time prevents an accidental larger-than-expected deletion, and gives you a documented expected scope to compare against after the fact — which is exactly what Step 3's post-deletion check verifies against.

questions.q: In Step 3's cascade integrity check, what does a non-zero OrphanCount at any level actually mean?
choices: The cascade did not complete fully at that level — child rows were left behind referencing a now-deleted parent, and remediation is needed
The deletion failed completely and no rows were removed
It means the check itself has a bug
A non-zero count is always expected and can be ignored
questions.right: Exactly — zero across every level is the only "cascade fully worked" result. Any non-zero count is a direct signal that some layer of the hierarchy was left with dangling references the cascade never reached.
questions.wrong: Zero at every level means the cascade genuinely removed everything it should have. A non-zero count at ANY level — even just one layer down — means the cascade stopped short somewhere, leaving orphaned child rows behind. Per the lesson, that's exactly the situation from the scenario: the GDPR deletion ticket was closed as complete when it actually wasn't, until an audit found the leftover OrderItems six weeks later.

G03-T08.close: You've now got a repeatable way to actually verify a cascade delete worked, instead of trusting "no error was thrown" as proof. Missing Mandatory Relationship is next — the last lesson in this group, and it circles back to a distinction you'll want to have crisp: relationships that were never set at all versus ones that broke later.

G03-T09.open: Last lesson in Referential Integrity. This one is about a relationship the business calls mandatory, that the schema quietly allows to not exist at all.

questions.q: The lesson combines two distinct failure modes into one check for a mandatory relationship. What are they?
choices: CustomerID is NULL (the relationship was never set), and CustomerID has a value but doesn't match any row in Customers (an orphan)
CustomerID is too long, and CustomerID contains special characters
The order was placed on a weekend, and the order total is zero
The customer's name is misspelled, and their email is invalid
questions.right: Exactly — both are ways a mandatory relationship can fail to actually exist: the field was left completely empty, or it was filled in with a value that points nowhere real. Case 3's CASE expression catches both in a single pass.
questions.wrong: A mandatory relationship can be violated two different ways: the FK column is left NULL entirely (nobody set it), or it's populated but with a value that has no matching row in the parent table (an orphan). Both mean the order effectively has no valid customer attached — Case 3 in the lesson checks for both conditions together with a single CASE expression.

questions.q: Why does the lesson call a nullable FK column a 'schema smell' when the business rule says the relationship is mandatory?
choices: A nullable column tells the schema "this relationship is optional," directly contradicting a business rule that says it's required — that mismatch means the database won't enforce what the business actually needs
Nullable columns always cause SQL Server performance problems
It's purely a stylistic preference with no functional consequence
NULL values are illegal in SQL Server and this is a bug
questions.right: Exactly — the schema and the business rule are telling two different stories. Whenever that mismatch exists, violations accumulate over time because nothing in the database itself is stopping them.
questions.wrong: If the real rule is "every Order must have a Customer," the column should be NOT NULL — that's how you'd tell the schema the relationship is required. Leaving it nullable means the schema is silently saying "optional" while the business says "mandatory." That contradiction is exactly why violations build up over time: nothing at the database level is actually enforcing what the business requires.

questions.q: The lesson explicitly distinguishes this lesson from G03-T02 (Dangling Reference). What's the actual difference between the two?
choices: G03-T02 covers a parent that was valid and later deleted; G03-T09 covers a relationship that was never set or never valid to begin with — same SQL pattern (NOT EXISTS), different root cause and remediation
G03-T02 only applies to Customers, G03-T09 only applies to Products
There is no real difference between the two lessons
G03-T09 uses a completely different SQL technique than G03-T02
questions.right: Exactly — same detection query, genuinely different story behind the data, which is exactly the same shape of distinction as orphan vs. dangling reference back in G03-T01/T02. Two lessons in this group, same underlying lesson: the SQL for finding a broken relationship often can't tell you why it's broken.
questions.wrong: Per the lesson's own comparison: G03-T02 (Dangling Reference) is about a parent that existed and was later deleted — the relationship was valid once. G03-T09 is about a relationship that was either never set (NULL) or never valid at all from the moment it was created. The SQL overlap is real (both lean on NOT EXISTS), but the root cause — and therefore the correct fix — is different in each case.

G03-T09.close: That's the full Referential Integrity group — nine lessons, and you've gone from a single broken FK all the way through self-referencing loops, cross-database boundaries, and cascades that only partially worked. The throughline across all nine: a foreign key constraint, when it exists at all, only ever answers "does the parent exist" — never "is the relationship still meaningful." Everything else needs a query like the ones you just worked through. Strong finish to this group.

G04-T01.open: Group 4: Format/Pattern — the biggest group in Data Validation, so we'll take it in two sittings. This half starts with the field everyone recognizes instantly when it's broken: email.

questions.q: The pattern `%_@__%.__%` is used to validate email structure. What does it actually require?
choices: At least one character before the @, at least two characters after it, a literal dot, and at least two more characters after that dot
Exactly one character before and after the @ symbol
The email must contain no more than 10 characters total
The domain must be a real, resolvable domain name
questions.right: Exactly — read left to right: one-or-more chars, @, two-or-more chars (domain start), a dot, two-or-more chars (TLD). That's the minimum shape a real email needs, without claiming to know if the domain is real.
questions.wrong: Breaking the pattern down piece by piece: `%_` means one or more characters before the @. `@` is the literal symbol. `__%` means at least two characters after it (the domain). `.` is a literal dot. The final `__%` means at least two more characters (the TLD). Together that's the minimum structural shape of a real email — nothing about whether the domain actually exists.

questions.q: Why does the lesson suggest `LEN(Email) - LEN(REPLACE(Email, '@', '')) > 1` as sometimes better than `Email LIKE '%@%@%'` for catching multiple @ symbols?
choices: It's more readable and correctly handles three or more @ symbols, not just exactly two
LIKE cannot detect the @ symbol at all
REPLACE is faster than every other string function in SQL Server
The two approaches check completely different things
questions.right: Right — the REPLACE-and-subtract trick directly counts occurrences, so it scales cleanly to 3, 4, or any number of @ symbols, where the LIKE pattern only really names the two-@ case explicitly.
questions.wrong: `LIKE '%@%@%'` explicitly checks for the two-@ case. The REPLACE-based version removes every @ and compares the length difference to the original — that difference IS the @ count, so it correctly flags 3, 4, or more @ symbols without needing a longer and longer LIKE pattern for each additional case.

questions.q: The lesson lists several things this SQL-only email validation does NOT catch. What are they?
choices: Whether the domain actually exists, disposable email providers, unicode characters, and RFC 5321 length limits
Whether the @ symbol is present
Whether the email contains spaces
Whether the email is NULL
questions.right: Exactly — this check is entirely structural. It's a strong first filter, but genuine deliverability needs a DNS lookup or an external verification API, which is outside what SQL can do.
questions.wrong: The lesson is explicit about the boundary: SQL LIKE validation checks *shape*, not *reality*. It can't tell you if a domain actually exists (needs DNS), catch disposable providers, handle unicode addresses, or enforce RFC 5321's exact length limits (64 chars local-part, 255 total). Those need application-layer or external-API validation — SQL structural checks are the first filter, not the last.

G04-T01.close: Structural pattern matching is the whole toolkit for this group — it tells you the shape is right, never that the meaning is right. Phone Number Format is next, where "right shape" turns out to vary by country in ways email doesn't.

G04-T02.open: Phone numbers are worse than email for one specific reason: there's no universal symbol like @ to anchor on. Every convention — spaces, dashes, parentheses, country codes — is technically valid somewhere.

questions.q: Why does the query strip out `+`, `-`, spaces, and parentheses before counting the digits in a phone number?
choices: It lets length be validated independently of whatever formatting convention the data entry used — the digit count is what actually matters for E.164 range checking
SQL Server cannot count characters in a string that contains punctuation
It converts the phone number into a valid E.164 number automatically
Stripping characters makes the LIKE pattern run faster
questions.right: Exactly — 07911 123456 and 07911123456 are the same number with different formatting. Stripping first means the length check works regardless of which formatting convention was used to enter it.
questions.wrong: A phone number can be legitimately written with or without spaces, dashes, or parentheses — `07911 123456` and `07911123456` are the same number. Stripping those characters out first means the digit-count check (E.164 allows 7-15 digits) works the same way regardless of which formatting style the data entry used, instead of needing a separate length rule for every formatting variant.

questions.q: What does the pattern `LIKE '%[^0-9+() -]%'` catch?
choices: Any character that is never valid in a phone field — letters, @, #, *, commas, and similar
Phone numbers that are exactly 10 digits long
Only phone numbers from outside the UK
Phone numbers containing a plus sign
questions.right: Right — the `[^...]` bracket means "not in this set." Anything outside digits, +, (, ), space, and - gets flagged, which is exactly the set of characters that should never appear in a phone field.
questions.wrong: The `[^0-9+() -]` bracket expression means "any character NOT in this set." The allowed set here is digits, +, parentheses, spaces, and hyphens — the characters that legitimately show up in phone number formatting. Anything else (letters, @, #, commas) trips this check, catching garbage values like "call me on mobile" or "N/A".

questions.q: Why does the lesson say SQL can verify a phone number's plausibility but not its validity?
choices: A US number and a UK mobile can share the exact same digit count while having completely different real structures — right length doesn't mean right format for that country
SQL cannot count digits in a phone number at all
Phone numbers are always exactly 10 digits regardless of country
Validity checking requires a network connection, which plausibility checking also requires
questions.right: Exactly — length is a weak proxy for correctness. Two numbers can pass the exact same digit-count check while belonging to totally different national numbering plans.
questions.wrong: The lesson's own example: a 10-digit US number and a 10-digit UK mobile pass the same digit-count check but follow completely different real structures. SQL can confirm "this has a plausible length and no letters" — plausibility. It cannot confirm "this is a real number formatted correctly for its country" — validity. That needs country-specific format rules, which is a much bigger job than one generic check.

G04-T02.close: Same lesson as email, one level harder: length and character-set checks get you plausibility, never certainty. Postcode / ZIP Code Format is next, where the country-specific angle becomes the entire point of the lesson.

G04-T03.open: This one makes the country-specific problem from the last lesson unavoidable — a UK postcode and a US ZIP code don't just look different, they follow completely different structural rules.

questions.q: Why must the query filter `WHERE Country = 'UK'` before applying the UK postcode LIKE patterns, rather than checking all postcodes against all patterns at once?
choices: Mixing UK and US postcode patterns in one check produces false positives — a valid US ZIP could accidentally look invalid against UK rules, or vice versa
SQL Server cannot filter by Country and PostalCode in the same query
UK and US postcodes always have exactly the same length
Filtering by country makes the query run in a different database
questions.right: Exactly — a country-specific format rule only makes sense applied to that country's data. Apply it universally and you'll flag correct US ZIPs as broken UK postcodes, and vice versa.
questions.wrong: The lesson is direct about this: "country-specific patterns should be separated." A UK postcode pattern has no idea what a valid US ZIP looks like, and applying it to US records would flag perfectly valid ZIPs as broken. Filtering by Country first means each pattern only ever gets applied to the data it was actually designed for.

questions.q: What's the practical difference between LIKE and PATINDEX that the lesson highlights?
choices: LIKE returns a true/false match; PATINDEX returns the actual position of the first invalid character, useful when you need to show exactly where a violation occurs
PATINDEX only works on numeric columns
LIKE is always faster than PATINDEX for any check
They are functionally identical with no real difference
questions.right: Right — LIKE tells you yes-or-no. PATINDEX tells you yes-or-no AND exactly where. That extra detail matters when a human needs to actually go fix the specific character that's wrong.
questions.wrong: LIKE is a boolean check — it tells you whether a pattern matches, nothing more. PATINDEX returns a number — the position of the first character that violates the pattern. That's genuinely more useful when you want to tell someone exactly *where* in the string the problem is, not just that a problem exists somewhere.

questions.q: Why does validating a single UK postcode require several different LIKE patterns OR'd together, instead of just one?
choices: UK postcodes have multiple valid outward-code shapes (AN, ANN, AAN, AANN, ANA, AANA) — a single fixed pattern can't cover all of them at once
UK postcodes are randomly generated with no consistent structure
LIKE only supports checking one character position at a time regardless of the pattern
It's an arbitrary stylistic choice with no structural reason
questions.right: Exactly — LIKE patterns are position-by-position and fixed-length, so each of the six real outward-code shapes needs its own explicit pattern. There's no way to express "2 or 4 letters" in a single LIKE expression.
questions.wrong: UK postcodes genuinely have six different valid outward-code shapes depending on the area (single letter + digit, double letter + digit, letter + digit + letter, and so on). Because LIKE patterns check fixed character positions with no "variable length" quantifier, each shape needs its own explicit pattern — which is why the query OR's together six separate LIKE checks instead of using just one.

G04-T03.close: You've now hit the real limitation of LIKE for this group: no quantifiers, so every valid shape needs its own explicit pattern. Date Format is next — where the danger isn't invalid data at all, it's data that looks perfectly valid and means the wrong thing.

G04-T04.open: This lesson is different from the others so far — the scary case here isn't a string that fails to parse, it's one that parses successfully into the WRONG date, silently.

questions.q: Why does the lesson insist on TRY_CAST/TRY_CONVERT instead of plain CAST/CONVERT when validating a column full of date strings?
choices: CAST throws an error and halts the entire query the moment it hits one unparseable value; TRY_CAST returns NULL for that row and lets the rest of the query keep running
TRY_CAST is simply a faster version of CAST with no functional difference
CAST cannot convert strings to DATE under any circumstances
TRY_CAST automatically fixes ambiguous dates
questions.right: Exactly — this is the whole reason TRY_ variants exist. One bad row with plain CAST kills the whole query; with TRY_CAST that one row just becomes NULL and everything else still runs.
questions.wrong: This is a hard practical distinction: plain `CAST(value AS DATE)` throws a runtime error the instant it meets a string it can't parse — the entire query stops. `TRY_CAST` returns NULL for that one row instead and keeps going, letting you validate every row in one pass rather than having the whole query die on the first bad value.

questions.q: Why is `01/02/2024` fundamentally ambiguous, and what does the lesson say is the only real fix?
choices: It's a valid date under both DD/MM/YYYY and MM/DD/YYYY conventions with different meanings each way — the only safe fix is standardizing all dates to ISO 8601 (YYYY-MM-DD) at the point of entry
It's ambiguous because the year is written with only 4 digits
SQL Server always interprets it as MM/DD/YYYY with no ambiguity
The fix is to delete any date matching this pattern
questions.right: Exactly — this isn't a parsing failure, it's a parsing *success* into two different possible dates. Since SQL Server has no way to know which convention was intended, the lesson's fix is prevention at the source: store dates in the one format that's never ambiguous.
questions.wrong: 01 and 02 are both valid day-or-month values, so `01/02/2024` genuinely means two different real dates depending on convention — 1 February or 2 January — and there's no way for SQL Server to guess which one is correct without external context. The lesson's answer isn't a smarter parsing trick, it's eliminating the ambiguity entirely: standardize everything to ISO 8601 (YYYY-MM-DD) at the point of entry, which reads the same way under every convention.

questions.q: What does the Step 4 pattern — COALESCE over several TRY_CONVERT calls with different style codes — actually accomplish?
choices: It attempts the most likely date format first and falls back through alternates, documenting which format code actually succeeded for each row
It always converts every date to the current date
It deletes rows that fail every conversion attempt
It only works for dates already in ISO 8601 format
questions.right: Right — COALESCE returns the first non-NULL value, so trying ISO first, then British, then US, then a fourth style means you get the best guess from whichever format actually worked, plus a record of which one it was.
questions.wrong: COALESCE returns the first non-NULL argument it's given. Chaining several TRY_CONVERT attempts — ISO, then British DD/MM/YYYY, then US MM/DD/YYYY, then DD-MM-YYYY — means the query tries the most likely format first and falls through to the next one only if that attempt failed. The companion CASE expression then records which specific format actually succeeded, which is essential for a migration where you need to know how much of the ambiguity was actually resolved.

G04-T04.close: Dates are the first lesson in this group where the failure mode is silent corruption, not an obvious error — worth remembering as the sharpest example of why "it parsed" isn't the same as "it parsed correctly." Numeric String Format is next, and it has the exact same ambiguity trap with commas instead of slashes.

G04-T05.open: Same shape of danger as the date lesson, different character. A comma in a number can mean two completely different things depending on which country wrote it.

questions.q: Why is `19,99` genuinely ambiguous in a way SQL cannot resolve on its own?
choices: It could be 19.99 written with a European decimal comma, or it could be 1,999 with the comma as a thousands separator — both are real conventions, and nothing in the string itself says which one applies
The comma is always a syntax error in SQL Server strings
SQL Server always interprets a comma as a decimal point automatically
It's only ambiguous if the column also contains letters
questions.right: Exactly — same shape of problem as the DD/MM date ambiguity: two real, valid conventions produce the same string with wildly different meanings. Resolving it needs to know the data's locale, which SQL has no way to infer.
questions.wrong: This mirrors the date-format ambiguity exactly: `19,99` is a perfectly valid European way of writing 19.99 (comma as decimal separator), AND it's a perfectly valid way of writing part of 1,999 (comma as thousands separator). The lesson is explicit that this must be resolved by knowing the data's locale — not by guessing in SQL, because guessing wrong is worse than not converting at all.

questions.q: The lesson's own Step 3 example shows `19,99` being cleaned into `1999` after naive comma-removal, producing a ParsedPrice of `1999.0000`. What does this demonstrate?
choices: Exactly the danger the Explanation warns about — blindly stripping the comma assumed it was a thousands separator, silently turning a real €19.99 price into a wildly wrong 1999, roughly 100x too high
That the cleaning logic in Step 3 is completely correct and needs no caution
That commas should never appear in any numeric column under any circumstances
That TRY_CAST always fails on values containing commas
questions.right: Exactly — this is a cautionary example built right into the lesson, not an endorsement. It shows precisely what "guessing wrong" costs: a price 100x too high, generated by code that ran without any error at all.
questions.wrong: This is the lesson demonstrating its own warning in action: if `19,99` actually meant 19.99 (European decimal), naively stripping the comma turns it into `1999` — a price roughly 100 times too high, and the conversion succeeds with no error thrown. It's a live example of exactly the locale-guessing danger the Explanation section warns about, not a recommended approach.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say to validate AFTER cleaning a numeric string, not just before?
choices: A string like '19.99 incl. VAT' still fails to cast to DECIMAL even after removing the currency symbol, because the trailing text is still there — cleaning one problem doesn't guarantee the value is now valid
Validating after cleaning is always unnecessary and wastes a query step
SQL Server automatically validates every value after any REPLACE function runs
Cleaning always produces a valid numeric value with no exceptions
questions.right: Right — cleaning one specific problem (a currency symbol) doesn't mean every problem is gone. "19.99 incl. VAT" still has trailing text after the £ is stripped, and only re-checking after cleaning catches that.
questions.wrong: The lesson's example: removing the £ from '£19.99' does leave a castable '19.99' — but removing the £ from '19.99 incl. VAT' still leaves '19.99 incl. VAT', which is still not a valid number. Cleaning addresses one specific pattern; it doesn't guarantee every other problem is gone too. Re-validating after cleaning is what actually confirms the value is now usable, not just less obviously broken.

G04-T05.close: The comma-ambiguity trap here is the same lesson as DD/MM dates, wearing different clothes — and worth remembering together. IBAN / Bank Account Number Format is next, where format rules get genuinely more complex: country-specific length, not just country-specific separators.

G04-T06.open: IBANs raise the stakes: 30+ countries, each with its own length and structure, plus a real cryptographic check-digit algorithm that SQL genuinely cannot compute on its own.

questions.q: Why does the query normalize the IBAN — strip spaces, convert to uppercase — before running any structural check at all?
choices: IBANs are often written with spaces for readability (GB29 NWBK...); validating the raw, unnormalized form would incorrectly flag a perfectly valid IBAN as wrong length or wrong pattern
Uppercase letters are invalid in a real IBAN
Normalizing an IBAN automatically verifies its check digits
SQL Server cannot compare strings that contain spaces under any circumstances
questions.right: Exactly — a spaced-out IBAN like 'GB29 NWBK...' is completely valid, just formatted for human readability. Checking length or pattern against the raw spaced version would wrongly reject it.
questions.wrong: People commonly write IBANs with spaces every 4 characters for readability — that's a valid, common convention, not an error. If you ran the length check against the raw string, a correct IBAN with spaces would fail for having the "wrong" length. Stripping spaces and uppercasing first means the structural checks are always applied to the normalized form, which is what actually determines validity.

questions.q: Why can't the real IBAN check-digit algorithm (mod-97) be directly computed with standard SQL Server integer arithmetic?
choices: The algorithm requires converting the rearranged IBAN into a number up to 34 digits long and taking it modulo 97 — SQL Server integers overflow at 19 digits, well short of that
SQL Server has no MOD or modulo function at all
The algorithm only works on IBANs shorter than 10 characters
Mod-97 is a made-up algorithm that doesn't actually exist
questions.right: Exactly — this is a genuine numeric limitation, not a missing feature. A 34-digit number is simply too large for SQL Server's native integer types, which is why the lesson says this specific check needs a CLR function or application code instead.
questions.wrong: The real IBAN check-digit rule (ISO 7064, mod-97-10) needs the rearranged IBAN converted into a number that can be up to 34 digits long, then taken modulo 97. SQL Server's native integer types overflow at 19 digits — nowhere near enough. That's a hard numeric ceiling, which is exactly why the lesson says this specific validation needs a CLR function or application-layer code rather than plain T-SQL.

questions.q: What does the lesson identify as the most reliable structural test available in plain SQL, short of the full check-digit algorithm?
choices: Whether the normalized IBAN's length matches the expected length for its declared country code (e.g. GB and DE both expect 22 characters, FR expects 27)
Whether the IBAN contains at least one number
Whether the IBAN is longer than 5 characters
Whether the IBAN was entered in lowercase
questions.right: Right — country-specific expected length is the strongest signal SQL can reasonably check without a full mod-97 implementation. It won't catch every typo, but it catches a large share of real errors cheaply.
questions.wrong: Since the full check-digit algorithm is out of reach for plain SQL, the lesson's practical fallback is comparing the normalized IBAN's actual length against the expected length for its declared country code — GB and DE should both be 22 characters, FR should be 27, and so on. It's not a complete validation, but it's the strongest structural signal available without a CLR function or external validator.

G04-T06.close: IBANs are the first lesson in this group where SQL genuinely hits a wall — some validation just isn't possible in plain T-SQL, and knowing where that wall is matters as much as knowing the patterns that work. National ID / Tax Reference Format is next, with a similar "structure isn't the whole story" theme.

G04-T07.open: This one makes explicit something the last few lessons hinted at: getting the shape right is necessary, but for some fields it's genuinely not enough.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say a correct LIKE pattern match is 'necessary but not sufficient' for validating a UK National Insurance Number?
choices: HMRC has additional business rules beyond the basic shape — forbidden first/second letters, forbidden two-letter prefixes, and a restricted suffix — that a structural pattern alone cannot express
LIKE patterns cannot check letters, only digits
NINOs don't actually have any defined structure at all
The pattern match is sufficient and the extra checks are unnecessary
questions.right: Exactly — `AB123456C` can match the basic AA999999A shape perfectly while still being invalid, because HMRC forbids specific letters and prefixes that a generic pattern has no way to know about.
questions.wrong: The LIKE pattern `[A-Z][A-Z][0-9][0-9][0-9][0-9][0-9][0-9][A-D]` confirms the NINO has the right basic shape — but HMRC layers extra rules on top: certain first letters are forbidden (D, F, I, Q, U, V), certain second letters are forbidden, certain two-letter prefix combinations are banned entirely, and the suffix must be A-D. A value can satisfy the shape and still violate one of these business rules, which is why they need separate checks after the structural one passes.

questions.q: Why does the query select both the original NationalID and the normalized (no-spaces) version, rather than just overwriting with the normalized form?
choices: The normalized form is used for validation and storage consistency, but the original form may still be needed for display purposes or an audit trail
SQL Server requires every column to be selected in both forms
The normalized form is always invalid and only exists for comparison
There is no real reason — it's an arbitrary stylistic choice
questions.right: Right — validation needs the clean, consistent form, but the original as entered can matter for showing the user what they typed or for an audit record of the raw input.
questions.wrong: The lesson notes this directly: normalize (strip spaces) for validation because that's the consistent form the pattern rules expect, but keep the original around too, since it may be needed for display purposes or an audit trail of exactly what was entered. Validating on one form doesn't mean you have to discard the other.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend also running a uniqueness check on NINOs, in addition to format validation?
choices: A NINO can have a perfectly valid format and still be duplicated across two different employee records — that's a different class of error format validation alone can't catch
Format validation and uniqueness checking are the exact same SQL query
NINOs are never used as identifiers, so uniqueness is irrelevant
Running both checks together is required by SQL Server syntax rules
questions.right: Exactly — format-valid and unique are two independent properties. A NINO can pass every structural and business rule check and still be accidentally assigned to two different people, which format validation was never designed to catch.
questions.wrong: The lesson connects this directly back to the Uniqueness group: if NINOs are used as a unique identifier, a value can be perfectly well-formatted (right shape, right prefix rules, right suffix) and still be a duplicate assigned to two different employees. That's a completely separate failure mode from format — one checks "is this shaped correctly," the other checks "does this appear more than once," and you need both.

G04-T07.close: This lesson is the clearest statement yet of a theme running through this whole group: structure and business rules are two different checks, and passing one says nothing about the other. URL / URI Format is next, applying the same idea to web addresses.

G04-T08.open: URLs bring back the "SQL can check shape, not reality" theme from the very first lesson in this group — but with a genuinely dangerous twist: a single invisible character can break HTTP routing entirely.

questions.q: Why can SQL only verify a URL's structure, not whether the URL actually works?
choices: Confirming a URL resolves to a real, reachable page requires making an actual HTTP request — something SQL cannot do; it can only check the shape (scheme, domain, dot)
SQL Server has a built-in HTTP client that is simply disabled by default
URLs cannot be stored as strings in SQL Server
Structural validation and resolution checking are exactly the same thing
questions.right: Exactly — this is the same shape-vs-reality boundary from the email lesson, applied to URLs. Format validation and link checking (does it return a 200) are two different tools for two different questions.
questions.wrong: Format validation confirms a URL LOOKS like a URL — has a scheme, a domain with a dot, no broken characters. Confirming it actually WORKS — returns a 200 status instead of a 404 — requires making a real HTTP request, which is entirely outside what a SQL query can do. The lesson is explicit that both checks matter but need different tools: SQL for structure, a separate link-checking process for reachability.

questions.q: Why does the lesson treat a raw space inside a URL as a serious structural problem, not just untidy formatting?
choices: A raw space breaks HTTP routing because space is a delimiter in the HTTP request line — a valid URL must have spaces percent-encoded as %20 instead
Spaces are cosmetically ugly but have no functional effect on a URL
SQL Server cannot store any string containing a space character
A space in a URL always causes a syntax error when the query runs
questions.right: Right — this isn't a style preference, it's a protocol-level problem. HTTP itself uses space as a delimiter, so an unencoded space in a URL can genuinely break how the request gets parsed and routed.
questions.wrong: This is a real functional problem, not cosmetics: the HTTP protocol uses a raw space character as a delimiter within the request line itself. A URL with an unencoded space in it can break how a server parses the request. The correct representation is the percent-encoded form (%20) — which is exactly why `LIKE '% %'` is flagged as a real structural violation, not just messy formatting.

questions.q: Why does the lesson's Step 5 separately count HTTP vs HTTPS URLs, rather than treating any working scheme as equally fine?
choices: HTTP vs HTTPS is a security concern on top of being a format concern — an HTTP URL is structurally valid but represents a security downgrade worth flagging to the security team
HTTP URLs are always structurally invalid and should be deleted
SQL Server cannot distinguish between the two schemes
It's purely a cosmetic count with no operational purpose
questions.right: Exactly — this is a case where format-valid and business-acceptable diverge. An HTTP URL passes every structural check and still represents something worth separately tracking and eventually fixing.
questions.wrong: An `http://` URL is perfectly valid structurally — it has a scheme, a domain, everything the format check requires. But every externally-facing URL should use HTTPS for security reasons, so the lesson deliberately tracks the two separately: format-valid doesn't mean security-acceptable, and Step 5 surfaces that gap as its own metric for the security team to act on.

G04-T08.close: URLs bring the shape-vs-reality theme back explicitly, plus a genuine security angle on top of pure format. Currency Amount Format is next — a lesson where the number itself can be perfectly valid and still be wrong by a factor of 100.

G04-T09.open: This lesson's danger doesn't come from an invalid character or a bad shape at all — every value here is a perfectly legal number. The problem is which unit it's actually measured in.

questions.q: What does a suspiciously large amount (e.g. over £100,000 for what should be an everyday transaction) most likely indicate, per the lesson?
choices: A minor-unit import error — the source system sent the amount in pence/cents but it was never divided by 100 before being stored as if it were pounds/dollars
The customer made an unusually large legitimate purchase
A rounding error in the last decimal place
The Amount column has the wrong data type
questions.right: Exactly — this is the scenario's core failure mode. Processor B's minor-unit amounts (pence) landed in the same column as major-unit amounts (pounds) with no conversion, making every one of those values look 100x too large.
questions.wrong: Per the scenario: one payment processor sent amounts in minor units (pence/cents — £19.99 becomes 1999), and that conversion to major units (dividing by 100) never happened. A value that's implausibly large relative to a normal transaction range is the tell-tale sign of exactly this kind of unit mismatch, not a genuinely huge legitimate purchase.

questions.q: What does the check `Amount <> ROUND(Amount, 2)` actually test for?
choices: Whether the amount has more precision than 2 decimal places — meaning rounding it to 2dp would actually change its value
Whether the amount is negative
Whether the amount is exactly zero
Whether the amount is stored as a string instead of a number
questions.right: Right — if rounding to 2dp doesn't change the value, the two sides are equal and nothing is flagged. If they differ, the original had real precision beyond 2dp that got lost in rounding — exactly what the check is hunting for.
questions.wrong: If an amount already has 2 or fewer decimal places, rounding it to 2dp gives back the exact same value — the two sides of the `<>` are equal, so nothing is flagged. If the amount has more precision (like 19.990000), rounding it changes the value, and the inequality catches that. This is a direct test for "does this value carry more precision than the currency should have."

questions.q: Why can't a single precision rule (like "always 2 decimal places") apply across every currency in the table?
choices: Different currencies have genuinely different decimal precision by definition — JPY uses 0 decimal places, GBP/USD use 2, and some cryptocurrencies use 8 or more
SQL Server only supports 2 decimal places for any DECIMAL column
All currencies actually use exactly the same precision, so one rule is fine
Precision rules only matter for negative amounts
questions.right: Exactly — precision itself is currency-specific, not a universal constant. Applying a flat 2dp rule to JPY (which should be whole numbers) or crypto (which needs far more precision) would flag perfectly correct values as errors.
questions.wrong: The lesson lists real examples: Japanese Yen has 0 decimal places by definition (there's no such thing as half a yen in normal transactions), GBP and USD use 2, Bahraini Dinar uses 3, and cryptocurrencies commonly use 8 or more. A single hard-coded "always 2dp" rule would incorrectly flag valid JPY amounts and incorrectly pass invalid crypto amounts — precision has to be looked up per currency, not assumed globally.

G04-T09.close: This is the sharpest example yet of a value being individually valid and collectively wrong — every number here parses fine, and the problem only shows up when you know what unit it's supposed to be in. IP Address Format is next, back to more familiar structural territory.

G04-T10.open: Back to structural validation, with a genuinely clever trick: reusing a function built for something completely different because it happens to fit the shape perfectly.

questions.q: Why is PARSENAME — a function designed for four-part object names like server.database.schema.table — a natural fit for validating an IPv4 address?
choices: An IPv4 address is also exactly four dot-separated parts, so PARSENAME works identically on it and returns NULL automatically if there aren't exactly 4 parts
PARSENAME was specifically built by Microsoft for IP address validation
PARSENAME only works on numeric strings, which is why it fits IP addresses
IP addresses and object names use a completely different separator character
questions.right: Exactly — it's a repurposed tool, not a coincidence. PARSENAME just extracts dot-separated segments and hands back NULL if the count is wrong, which happens to be exactly the shape of an IPv4 address.
questions.wrong: PARSENAME's actual job is splitting a four-part dotted name into its segments — but an IPv4 address is coincidentally the exact same shape: four dot-separated parts. Feed it an IP address and PARSENAME extracts each octet the same way it would extract a table name, and critically, it returns NULL automatically if there aren't exactly four parts — which doubles as a free structural check.

questions.q: Why is `LIKE '%.%.%.%'` alone not enough to fully validate an IPv4 address?
choices: It confirms there are four dot-separated parts, but says nothing about whether each part is actually a valid number between 0 and 255
LIKE cannot detect dots in a string at all
This pattern only matches IPv6 addresses, not IPv4
It's actually sufficient on its own and no further check is needed
questions.right: Right — this is exactly the structure-vs-range gap the lesson names directly: 192.168.999.1 passes this LIKE check perfectly while having an octet value that's completely invalid.
questions.wrong: The lesson gives the exact counter-example: `192.168.999.1` passes `LIKE '%.%.%.%'` — it genuinely has four dot-separated parts — but 999 is not a valid octet value (max is 255). LIKE confirms structure only; PARSENAME plus TRY_CAST is what's needed on top to confirm each individual octet actually falls in the valid 0-255 range.

questions.q: Why would a private IP range (10.x.x.x, 192.168.x.x) showing up as the SourceIP in a public-facing authentication log be worth investigating?
choices: It may indicate a reverse proxy not forwarding the real client IP, internal testing traffic leaking into production logs, or a misconfigured logging pipeline
Private IP ranges are always invalid IPv4 addresses
It always means the log data has been tampered with maliciously
Private IPs cannot technically appear in any database column
questions.right: Exactly — a private IP in a public-facing log isn't a format error, it's a signal something upstream is misconfigured. The lesson names three plausible causes, none of which is "the IP itself is invalid."
questions.wrong: A private IP address is perfectly valid as an IP address — the issue is context, not format. If it's showing up as the source of a public-facing authentication attempt, that's suspicious because internet traffic shouldn't originate from a private range. The lesson names three real possible causes: a reverse proxy failing to forward the actual client IP, internal test traffic mixed into production logs, or a genuinely misconfigured logging pipeline.

G04-T10.close: The PARSENAME trick is a nice reminder that a tool built for one job can solve a structurally-identical problem in a completely different domain. Product Code / SKU Format is next — a case where the organization defines its own structure from scratch.

G04-T11.open: Unlike email or IP addresses, this format isn't a universal standard — it's a rule the organization made up itself. Which means the validation has to encode business decisions, not just general structure.

questions.q: Why is a fixed-length LIKE pattern (like `[A-Z][A-Z][A-Z]-[A-Z][A-Z][A-Z]-[0-9][0-9][0-9][0-9][0-9][0-9]`) well suited to validating a SKU specifically?
choices: A SKU has a fixed total length and fixed-length segments, so each character position can be explicitly validated, making the rule precise and easy to read position by position
LIKE patterns can only be used on columns shorter than 20 characters
SKUs never contain any digits, only letters
Fixed-length patterns are required by SQL Server syntax for any VARCHAR column
questions.right: Exactly — when every character position has a known, fixed rule (3 letters, hyphen, 3 letters, hyphen, 6 digits), a LIKE pattern can spell that out explicitly and precisely, position by position.
questions.wrong: A SKU like `ELC-MOB-000042` has a completely fixed shape: 3 letters, a hyphen, 3 more letters, another hyphen, then exactly 6 digits. Because every position has a known, fixed rule, a LIKE pattern can validate each position explicitly and precisely — this is exactly the situation where LIKE patterns are the most reliable, since there's no ambiguity about length or position to worry about.

questions.q: Why does Step 2 decompose the ProductCode into separate named segments (CategoryCode, SubCategoryCode, SequenceNumber) instead of just reporting a single 'pattern mismatch' message?
choices: It produces a specific, actionable error message (e.g. 'Sub-category: must be 3 uppercase letters') instead of a vague one, which is essential when someone actually needs to go fix the data
SQL Server requires every LIKE pattern to be broken into separate segments to run at all
Decomposing the code automatically corrects it to the right format
It has no practical benefit over a single pattern-mismatch message
questions.right: Right — "pattern mismatch" tells you something's wrong. "Sub-category: must be 3 uppercase letters" tells you exactly what and where, which is what an import team actually needs to fix real data.
questions.wrong: A generic "pattern mismatch" message tells you something is wrong but not what. By checking each segment separately — category letters, first hyphen, sub-category letters, second hyphen, sequence digits — the query can say exactly which piece failed and why, which the lesson calls "essential when the import team needs to fix the data." Specificity turns a vague error into an actionable one.

questions.q: Why is a code like `ZZZ-ZZZ-000001` — which passes the structural LIKE pattern perfectly — still potentially wrong?
choices: The LIKE pattern only validates structure (3 letters, hyphen, 3 letters, hyphen, 6 digits) — it says nothing about whether 'ZZZ' is actually an approved category code from the organization's real list
ZZZ is a reserved keyword in SQL Server that always causes an error
Six-digit sequences starting with 000001 are never valid
The pattern actually rejects this code, so it wouldn't pass in the first place
questions.right: Exactly — this is structure vs. semantics again, the same theme from the NINO lesson. ZZZ is structurally three uppercase letters, which is all the LIKE pattern checks. Whether ZZZ is an actual approved category is a completely separate business-rule question.
questions.wrong: `ZZZ-ZZZ-000001` genuinely satisfies the structural rule — three letters, hyphen, three letters, hyphen, six digits. But whether 'ZZZ' is one of the organization's real, approved category codes (ELC, CLO, FUR, etc.) is a business rule the structural pattern has no way to check. That's exactly why Step 3 adds a separate lookup against the approved category list — structure and semantics are two different questions.

G04-T11.close: Same structure-vs-semantics idea as NINOs, applied to a code the business invented itself rather than a national standard. Case Convention Violation is next — a different kind of format problem entirely, where the characters are all correct and only their capitalization is wrong.

G04-T12.open: New angle entirely — every character in these values is technically correct. The only thing wrong is which case it's in, and that turns out to be enough to break deduplication completely.

questions.q: How does the test `FirstName = UPPER(FirstName)` correctly detect an ALL-CAPS value?
choices: If a string is already entirely uppercase, converting it to uppercase again produces an identical string, so the comparison is true only when the original was already all caps
UPPER() always returns a different string than its input, so the comparison is always false
This test only works on strings shorter than 10 characters
It checks whether the string contains any letters at all
questions.right: Exactly — UPPER() is idempotent on already-uppercase text, so the comparison only comes back true when nothing changed, which only happens when the original was already fully uppercase.
questions.wrong: If `FirstName` is 'JOHN', then `UPPER(FirstName)` is also 'JOHN' — no change, so the comparison is true. If `FirstName` is 'John', `UPPER(FirstName)` becomes 'JOHN' — different from the original, so the comparison is false. The test only comes back true in the specific case where uppercasing the string didn't change anything, which means it was already fully uppercase.

questions.q: Why does the Title Case approximation formula (`UPPER(LEFT(name,1)) + LOWER(SUBSTRING(name,2,...))`) fail on a name like MCDONALD?
choices: It only uppercases the very first letter and lowercases everything else, so MCDONALD becomes Mcdonald instead of the correct McDonald with an internal capital D
The formula only works on names shorter than 5 characters
SUBSTRING cannot process names containing the letter C
MCDONALD is not a real name and would be rejected entirely
questions.right: Right — the formula has no concept of internal capitalization rules. It blindly applies "first letter up, everything else down," which is wrong for names like McDonald, MacArthur, or O'Brien that need a capital somewhere in the middle.
questions.wrong: The formula is deliberately simple: capitalize position 1, lowercase everything from position 2 onward. For a straightforward name like 'john' → 'John' that works fine. But 'MCDONALD' has a legitimate internal capital (the D in McDonald) that this formula has no way to know about — it just sees "everything after position 1" and lowercases it all, producing 'Mcdonald' instead of the correct 'McDonald'.

questions.q: Why do codes (like country or status) and personal names follow opposite case conventions, and why does that matter for validation?
choices: Codes are conventionally ALL CAPS (GB, ACTIVE) while names are conventionally Title Case (John) — so the SAME check ("is this all uppercase?") means something completely different depending on which column type it's applied to
There is no real difference and both should use the exact same validation rule
Country codes are always exactly 2 characters, which is unrelated to case
Names should always be stored in ALL CAPS for consistency with codes
questions.right: Exactly — the SAME test (all-uppercase) is a PASS for a country code and a FAIL for a person's name. Applying one universal case rule across every text column would get half of them backwards.
questions.wrong: Country codes and status values are conventionally ALL CAPS ('GB', 'ACTIVE') — that's correct and expected. Personal names are conventionally Title Case ('John') — ALL CAPS there is the violation. This means "is this value all uppercase" is a PASS condition for one column type and a FAIL condition for another — you can't apply one blanket case rule across every text column, you have to know which convention that specific column is supposed to follow.

G04-T12.close: Case conventions are a reminder that "correct" depends entirely on what kind of value a column holds — the same test flips from pass to fail depending on context. Leading/Trailing Whitespace is next, the most invisible format problem in this entire group.

G04-T13.open: This might be the sneakiest lesson in the whole group — the bug is a character you cannot see, in a place most query tools won't even show you it's there.

questions.q: Why does `Email <> LTRIM(RTRIM(Email))` correctly detect whitespace padding?
choices: If a string has no leading or trailing spaces, trimming it produces an identical string, so the comparison is only true when trimming actually removed something
LTRIM and RTRIM always return an empty string
This comparison only works on columns shorter than 50 characters
It detects whitespace anywhere in the string, not just at the edges
questions.right: Exactly — same idempotence idea as the case-check lesson, applied to whitespace instead of case. Trimming a clean string changes nothing; trimming a padded one does, and that difference is exactly what the comparison catches.
questions.wrong: If `Email` is 'john@example.com' with no padding, trimming it gives back the exact same string — the comparison is false, nothing flagged. If `Email` is ' john@example.com' with a leading space, trimming removes that space, producing a shorter string that's now different from the original — the comparison is true. The test only fires when trimming actually changed something, which only happens when there was padding to remove.

questions.q: Why are non-breaking spaces (CHAR 160) invisible to LTRIM and RTRIM specifically?
choices: LTRIM and RTRIM only strip the ASCII space character (CHAR 32) — CHAR 160 is a visually identical but technically different character that these functions don't touch
LTRIM and RTRIM only work on the first 10 characters of a string
Non-breaking spaces don't actually exist as real characters in text
CHAR 160 is automatically converted to CHAR 32 by SQL Server before any function runs
questions.right: Right — this is a specific, narrow gap: LTRIM/RTRIM target exactly one character code (32), and CHAR 160 looks identical to a human but is a completely different character that slides right past them.
questions.wrong: LTRIM and RTRIM are built to strip a specific character: ASCII space, CHAR 32. The non-breaking space (CHAR 160 — ` ` in HTML) looks visually identical to a regular space but is a different character code entirely, so these functions simply don't recognize it as something to trim. It sails through untouched, which is exactly why the lesson needs a separate CHAR(160) check in Step 3.

questions.q: What does Step 4 — a self-join comparing trimmed, lowercased email values — reveal that Step 1 alone would miss?
choices: Pairs of records that are stored as different values but represent the exact same entity once whitespace is removed — the root cause of the split-account scenario in the lesson
Records where the Email column is completely NULL
The total count of all customers in the table
Records where the email domain doesn't have a valid TLD
questions.right: Exactly — Step 1 tells you which individual rows have whitespace. Step 4 tells you something more specific and more actionable: which pairs of rows are secretly duplicates of each other because of that whitespace.
questions.wrong: Step 1 flags individual rows that have leading or trailing whitespace — useful, but it doesn't tell you the consequence. Step 4 joins the table to itself on the trimmed, lowercased email and finds pairs of rows that differ as stored but match once cleaned — which is exactly the split-account bug from the scenario: 'john@example.com' and ' john@example.com' as two separate customer records that are actually the same person.
