questions.wrong: The lesson gives three specific reasons: NOT EXISTS short-circuits on the first matching row (faster against large parent tables than scanning a full LEFT JOIN), it reads as a natural English statement ("where no parent exists"), and it handles NULL FK values more intuitively. LEFT JOIN / IS NULL remains useful when you also want to pull columns from the parent table for comparison — it's not that either is broken, just suited to slightly different needs.

questions.q: What's the key difference between a NULL foreign key and an orphan foreign key, as the lesson distinguishes them?
choices: A NULL FK may be a valid optional relationship or a data gap; an orphan FK always points to a record that doesn't exist and is always a data integrity failure
A NULL FK is always a critical error, while an orphan FK is always harmless
They are the same thing, just described with different terminology
A NULL FK only occurs in the Orders table, while an orphan FK only occurs in the Transactions table
questions.right: Right — the lesson draws this line clearly: NULL just means "no reference given," which can be perfectly legitimate. An orphan means "a reference was given, but it points at nothing" — that's never legitimate.
questions.wrong: The lesson separates these as two distinct failure modes: a NULL foreign key means the reference is simply absent — which could be a valid optional relationship (not every order needs a product yet) or could be a genuine data entry gap, context-dependent. An orphan foreign key, by contrast, means the reference *exists* but points to a record that isn't there — that's always a data integrity failure, with no legitimate interpretation, because the reference is actively wrong rather than just missing.

questions.q: What does an orphan rate above 10% typically suggest, compared to a rate under 1%?
choices: Above 10% suggests a systematic failure (a dropped constraint, an ETL loading children without parents, a large delete on one table); under 1% suggests isolated incidents like test records or migration artefacts
Above 10% means the query itself contains a syntax error
Under 1% means referential integrity is completely broken and requires an emergency fix
The percentage has no bearing on severity — only the absolute orphan count matters
questions.right: Right — the lesson's own severity classification draws exactly this line: a handful of stray records reads very differently from a tenth of the whole table being orphaned.
questions.wrong: The lesson's severity classification distinguishes these directly: below 1% suggests isolated incidents — developer test records, small migration artefacts — that don't point to a broken process. Above 10% suggests something systematic went wrong: a foreign key constraint was dropped, an ETL process loaded child records without their parents, or a large-scale delete hit only one side of a relationship. The percentage, not just the raw count, is what signals whether this is noise or a structural failure.

G13-T01.close: NOT EXISTS as the natural orphan-detection idiom, NULL vs orphan as two distinct failure modes, and orphan rate as a severity signal — referential integrity checking covered. Next: Circular Reference Detection, where a hierarchy loops back on itself.

G13-T02.open: Circular Reference Detection — a self-referencing hierarchy that loops is one of the few data quality problems that can actually crash a query, not just corrupt a report.

questions.q: Why is the path-string cycle guard (`CHARINDEX(...) = 0`) described as more robust than using a depth counter alone to prevent infinite recursion?
choices: A depth counter alone would incorrectly truncate valid deep hierarchies rather than actually detecting true cycles, while the path guard specifically checks whether a node has already been visited
CHARINDEX runs faster than any numeric comparison in SQL Server
A depth counter cannot be used inside a recursive CTE under any circumstances
The path guard eliminates the need for a MAXRECURSION safety limit entirely
questions.right: Right — a depth counter is a blunt instrument. It would stop a legitimately deep 15-level hierarchy at the same point it stops an infinite 3-node cycle, treating both the same way even though only one is actually broken.
questions.wrong: The lesson makes this comparison directly: a depth counter alone can only say "we've gone this many levels deep" — it can't distinguish a genuinely deep, valid hierarchy from an infinitely looping cycle, so it would incorrectly cut off valid deep trees at the same threshold that's meant to catch cycles. The path-string guard instead tracks which specific nodes have already been visited in this traversal, so it detects an actual repeat visit — a true cycle — rather than just a depth limit being reached.

questions.q: What happens by default in SQL Server if a recursive CTE traverses a genuine circular reference without a path guard in place?
choices: It hits SQL Server's default maximum recursion depth of 100 and throws an error, rather than looping forever
SQL Server automatically detects the cycle and silently skips the offending rows
The query returns an empty result set with no error or warning
SQL Server converts the recursive CTE into a non-recursive one automatically
questions.right: Right — SQL Server won't spin forever on its own. The default 100-level recursion cap turns an infinite loop into a hard error instead, though that's a safety net, not a substitute for actually detecting the cycle.
questions.wrong: The lesson states this explicitly: SQL Server's default maximum recursion depth is 100. Without a path guard, a genuine circular reference would hit this built-in limit and throw an error, rather than looping forever and hanging the server. It's a safety net against runaway queries, not a mechanism that identifies or fixes the cycle — that's what the path-string guard and cycle-detection logic are for.

questions.q: What are the three distinct structural problems the lesson identifies in self-referencing hierarchies?
choices: Self-loops (an employee is their own manager), multi-node cycles (A reports to B, who reports to C, who reports back to A), and dangling references (ManagerID points to a record that doesn't exist)
NULL values, duplicate rows, and empty strings
Missing indexes, slow queries, and locked tables
Incorrect data types, truncated strings, and rounding errors
questions.right: Right — three genuinely different shapes of the same underlying problem, each caught by a different step in the lesson: Step 1 for self-loops, Step 3 for multi-node cycles, Step 5 for dangling references.
questions.wrong: The lesson names these three specifically: self-loops, where ManagerID equals the employee's own EmployeeID (caught in Step 1); multi-node cycles, where following the chain eventually loops back to where it started, like A→B→C→A (caught in Step 3's recursive path-tracking); and dangling references, where ManagerID points to an EmployeeID that simply doesn't exist in the table at all (caught in Step 5). All three break a recursive traversal, but they need different detection logic because they're structurally different failures.

G13-T02.close: The robustness of path-tracking over depth limits, SQL Server's built-in recursion safety net, and the three distinct cycle types — circular reference detection covered. Next: Hierarchy Completeness and Depth Validation, checking whether the shape of the tree itself makes sense.

G13-T03.open: Hierarchy Completeness and Depth Validation — beyond just "does this reference exist," this technique asks whether the overall shape of the org chart is healthy: not too wide, not too deep, not fragmented.

questions.q: What are the three possible explanations the lesson gives for a hierarchy having multiple root nodes?
choices: Disconnected sub-trees loaded separately without a unifying parent, data quality errors (a root manager was deleted), or an intentional flat structure where several senior leaders report to no one
A SQL Server bug, a corrupted index, and a missing primary key constraint
Too many employees, too few departments, and an outdated schema
A JOIN fan-out, a duplicate row, and a NULL in the wrong column
questions.right: Right — three named possibilities, and the lesson is careful that not all of them are actually errors; one (the flat structure) can be intentional business design.
questions.wrong: The lesson lists these three specifically: disconnected sub-trees (different business units loaded separately without a single connecting parent), data quality errors (some employee's root manager record was deleted, orphaning their whole branch), or an intentional flat structure (several senior leaders genuinely report to no one). It flags multiple roots because they prevent correct depth calculation and hierarchy reporting regardless of which of these three caused it — but not every case is actually a mistake.

questions.q: Why might a manager with exactly 1 direct report be flagged as "potential hierarchy bloat" rather than simply accepted as a normal team structure?
choices: It could represent an intermediate management layer that adds an extra reporting hop without adding real organisational value
SQL Server treats any manager with fewer than 2 direct reports as an invalid record
A manager with 1 direct report always indicates a data entry error
It means the employee's ManagerID column contains a NULL value
questions.right: Right — it's a candidate for review, not a confirmed problem. A single-report manager could be a legitimate specialist role, but it could also just be unnecessary extra layering in the hierarchy.
questions.wrong: The lesson is careful to frame this as ambiguous, not automatically wrong: a manager with exactly 1 direct report could be legitimate structure (a specialist role that genuinely needs its own reporting line), or it could be hierarchy bloat — an intermediate layer inserted that adds a reporting hop without adding real organisational value. The flag exists to prompt a human review, since organisational design is ultimately a business decision the database alone can't settle.

questions.q: Why are "disconnected" employees (Step 3) invisible to any top-down hierarchy report, even though they still exist as rows in the Employees table?
choices: A top-down report works by traversing the hierarchy starting from the root(s), and a disconnected employee — by definition — cannot be reached by that traversal no matter how far it goes
Disconnected employees are automatically deleted from the table by a nightly cleanup job
SQL Server hides rows that fail a foreign key constraint from all SELECT queries
Disconnected employees only appear in reports generated on weekends
questions.right: Right — it's a structural consequence of how top-down traversal works, not a bug in any specific query. If a node can't be reached by walking down from a root, it will never appear in output built by that traversal, regardless of how the report is generated.
questions.wrong: The lesson's own definition makes this direct: a top-down hierarchy report works by starting at the root node(s) and traversing downward through parent-child links. A "disconnected" employee is, by the query's own definition, one that cannot be reached by that traversal — their root manager was deleted without reassigning their branch, or their ManagerID points to something that was never actually created as a root. The row still physically exists in the table; it's just structurally unreachable from any starting point the report knows to begin from.

G13-T03.close: Multiple roots as three distinct (not automatically bad) causes, single-report spans as a bloat candidate, and disconnected nodes as structurally unreachable rather than deleted — hierarchy completeness covered. Next: JSON Structure Validation, where schema drift inside a JSON column hides in plain sight.

G13-T04.open: JSON Structure Validation — a JSON column can stay perfectly syntactically valid while quietly using the wrong keys, and nothing about that will ever throw an error on its own.

questions.q: Why must `ISJSON()` be checked before relying on `JSON_VALUE()` to determine whether a key is genuinely present?
choices: JSON_VALUE() called on a syntactically invalid JSON string returns NULL rather than raising an error, so without ISJSON() first, you can't tell "key absent" apart from "the whole JSON document is broken"
JSON_VALUE() cannot be executed at all unless ISJSON() has already run earlier in the same script
ISJSON() automatically repairs any malformed JSON before JSON_VALUE() reads it
JSON_VALUE() only works on JSON arrays, never on JSON objects
questions.right: Right — the ambiguity is the whole reason ISJSON() has to run first. JSON_VALUE() gives you the same NULL result whether the document is broken or the key is just missing, so you need a separate check to tell those two very different problems apart.
questions.wrong: The lesson explains this precisely: calling JSON_VALUE() on a string that isn't valid JSON at all returns NULL rather than raising an error — the same NULL you'd get if the JSON were perfectly valid but the key was simply absent. Without checking ISJSON() first, a NULL from JSON_VALUE() is ambiguous between "this document is broken" and "this key doesn't exist in an otherwise fine document" — two very different problems that need different fixes.

questions.q: What's the difference in purpose between `JSON_VALUE()` and `JSON_QUERY()`?
choices: JSON_VALUE() extracts a scalar value (string, number, boolean); JSON_QUERY() extracts a nested object or array as a JSON fragment
JSON_VALUE() only works on the Orders table, while JSON_QUERY() only works on the Transactions table
JSON_QUERY() validates JSON syntax, while JSON_VALUE() extracts values — they cannot both be used in the same query
JSON_VALUE() is deprecated in SQL Server and JSON_QUERY() should always be used instead
questions.right: Right — different return types for different jobs. Reach for JSON_VALUE() when you want a single field's actual value; reach for JSON_QUERY() when the thing at that path is itself a nested structure.
questions.wrong: The lesson states this distinction directly: JSON_VALUE(col, '$.key') is for extracting an individual scalar value — a string, number, or boolean — as NVARCHAR. JSON_QUERY(col, '$.key') is for extracting something that's itself a nested object or array, returning it as a JSON fragment rather than trying to force it into a scalar. You'd use JSON_VALUE for something like `$.currency`, and JSON_QUERY for something like an embedded `$.address` object.

questions.q: Why can't `JSON_VALUE()` alone distinguish between "this key is absent from the document" and "this key exists but its value is explicitly `null`"?
choices: JSON_VALUE() returns NULL in both cases, so the two scenarios are indistinguishable from its return value alone — a JSON_QUERY() check or raw string inspection is needed to tell them apart
SQL Server does not allow JSON values to be explicitly set to null under any circumstances
JSON_VALUE() throws a runtime error whenever a key's value is explicitly null
A missing key and a null value are treated identically by definition and there is no meaningful difference between them
questions.right: Right — from JSON_VALUE()'s return value alone, you genuinely can't tell these apart; both come back as NULL. The lesson names the workaround (JSON_QUERY or raw string inspection) but also notes that for most purposes, treating both as "missing" is a fine simplification.
questions.wrong: The lesson states this ambiguity directly: JSON_VALUE() returns NULL both when a key is entirely absent from the document and when the key exists but its value is explicitly JSON `null`. To actually tell these apart, the lesson suggests using JSON_QUERY() and checking whether the returned fragment is the literal string "null", or inspecting the raw JSON text with something like `CHARINDEX('"source"', Metadata) > 0`. For most validation purposes, though, the lesson notes treating both cases as "missing" is an acceptable simplification.

G13-T04.close: The ISJSON-before-JSON_VALUE ordering, scalar vs nested extraction, and the absent-vs-null ambiguity — JSON structure validation covered. Next: Graph Connectivity and Orphan Node Detection, generalising from strict hierarchies to arbitrary networks.

G13-T05.open: Graph Connectivity and Orphan Node Detection — a hierarchy is really just a special, restricted kind of graph. This technique applies the same reachability thinking to relationships that don't have to form a strict tree.

questions.q: What defines an "isolated node" in this lesson's graph connectivity terms?
choices: Both in-degree and out-degree equal 0 — no edges point into the node, and no edges point out of it
The node has an in-degree of exactly 1 and any out-degree
The node's EmployeeID is NULL
The node has the maximum possible out-degree in the entire dataset
questions.right: Right — completely disconnected on both counts. No manager, no direct reports, no relationship to the rest of the graph at all.
questions.wrong: The lesson defines this precisely: in-degree is the count of edges pointing into a node, out-degree is the count of edges pointing out. An isolated node has both equal to 0 — in the management-hierarchy example, that means an employee with no ManagerID (in-degree 0) and no direct reports (out-degree 0), meaning they're entirely disconnected from the rest of the graph, not just at the edge of it.

questions.q: What does it mean for a set of nodes to form one "connected component", as defined in this lesson?
choices: Every node in the set is reachable from every other node in the set, treating the edges as undirected for this purpose
Every node in the set shares the exact same ManagerID value
The set contains exactly one root node and no leaf nodes
Every node in the set was created on the same date
questions.right: Right — reachability is the defining property, and it's checked in the undirected sense (ignoring which way each edge points), which is different from strict top-down hierarchy traversal.
questions.wrong: The lesson's definition is specific: a connected component is a set of nodes where every node is reachable from every other node, treated in an undirected sense (ignoring the direction each edge actually points). A tree — like a clean single-root management hierarchy — has exactly one connected component; a graph with disconnected sub-trees or isolated nodes has more than one. This is a more general concept than "reachable from the root," since it doesn't require a designated starting point.

questions.q: In Step 4's bipartite validation, what does it mean if a single OrderID shows more than one distinct CustomerID?
choices: A structural violation — each order is supposed to link exactly one customer to one product, so multiple customer values for one order suggests a JOIN fan-out or ETL error
It means the customer placed multiple orders on the same day, which is expected behaviour
It means the OrderID column contains a duplicate primary key, which SQL Server would normally prevent
It has no significance — OrderIDs are allowed to link to multiple customers by design
questions.right: Right — one order is supposed to map to exactly one customer. Seeing more than one for the same OrderID is a structural red flag, not a valid business scenario.
questions.wrong: The lesson frames this relationship as bipartite by design: each order should connect exactly one customer to one product. `COUNT(DISTINCT o.CustomerID) > 1` for a single OrderID violates that expected structure — the lesson attributes violations like this to ETL errors or JOIN multiplicities in the source data (for example, a JOIN that fanned out and duplicated rows), not to a legitimate business scenario where one order genuinely belongs to multiple customers.

G13-T05.close: Isolated nodes by zero in/out-degree, connected components as undirected reachability, and bipartite violations as ETL red flags — graph connectivity covered. Last one in this group: Nested Set and Adjacency List Consistency.

G13-T06.open: Last one in Hierarchical/Structural — Nested Set and Adjacency List Consistency. Two different ways to store the same tree, and this technique checks that a derived nested-set encoding actually agrees with the adjacency list it came from.

questions.q: Why can't lft/rgt values assigned as simple consecutive integers per row (`lft = 2n-1`, `rgt = 2n`, ordered by depth) ever demonstrate parent-child containment, no matter what data is loaded?
choices: Every node's own rgt is always exactly one more than its own lft by construction, so a containment check against those values can never fail regardless of the actual hierarchy structure
SQL Server does not allow lft and rgt to be computed using ROW_NUMBER() under any circumstances
Consecutive integers can only be used for hierarchies with fewer than 10 nodes
The values would always be identical for every employee, causing a primary key violation
questions.right: Right — that's exactly why this needed a real rewrite rather than a small fix. If rgt is always lft+1 by definition, no containment test run against those two numbers can ever meaningfully pass or fail — it's checking something that's true by construction, not by structure.
questions.wrong: The lesson's corrected version explains this directly: if lft and rgt are just consecutive integers derived from the same row number (`2n-1` and `2n`), then for every single row, rgt is always exactly lft+1 — guaranteed by how they're computed, completely independent of where that node actually sits in the tree. A containment check like "is this child's range inside its parent's range" tested against numbers with that property can never meaningfully fail, because it isn't actually testing the tree's real structure at all — it's testing an arithmetic fact that's true regardless of the data.

questions.q: What does the AncestorPath slash-count check in Step 1 verify?
choices: That the computed Depth value for each employee matches the number of separators in their accumulated ancestor path string, catching a recursive CTE error if they disagree
That every employee's FullName contains no special characters
That the AncestorPath string is shorter than 100 characters for every employee
That every employee has exactly one direct report
questions.right: Right — it's a self-consistency check on the recursive CTE's own output. The path string and the depth counter are built by two different pieces of the same query, so if they ever disagree, something in the recursion logic is wrong.
questions.wrong: The lesson explains this as an internal consistency check: the path string (like `'EMP-001/EMP-002/EMP-005'`) accumulates one segment per level of recursion, and the number of separators in it should always exactly equal the separately-tracked Depth counter. If they disagree, it means the recursive CTE's join condition or its depth initialization has a bug — the two values are computed by different parts of the same query, so agreement between them is a genuine correctness check, not just a formatting detail.

questions.q: According to the four nested-set consistency invariants listed in the lesson, what should the root node's lft and rgt values equal?
choices: lft = 1, and rgt = 2 × the total number of nodes in the hierarchy
lft and rgt should both equal 0 for the root node specifically
lft should equal the root's EmployeeID, and rgt should equal its Depth
The root node has no lft or rgt values at all, only its children do
questions.right: Right — the root's range has to span the entire tree, since every other node's range is nested inside it. lft = 1 (nothing precedes it) and rgt = 2N (it closes only after every other node has opened and closed).
questions.wrong: The lesson lists this as one of the four consistency invariants: the root has lft = 1 (since nothing in the entire tree comes before it opens) and rgt = 2 × total node count (since the root's range must contain every other node's range — the whole nested set is opened first and closed last). This is a direct consequence of the general rule that `rgt - lft + 1 = 2 × subtree size`, applied to the root, whose subtree is the entire tree.

G13-T06.close: Why naive consecutive pairs can never test real containment, the slash-count self-consistency check, and the root's lft=1/rgt=2N invariant — that closes out Hierarchical/Structural. Six techniques down: referential integrity, circular references, completeness and depth, JSON structure, graph connectivity, and nested set consistency.

G14-T01.open: Welcome to DW/SCD Specific — you've opened SCD Type 2 Gap and Overlap Detection, checking that a dimension's version history is contiguous and never double-covers a date. Three questions, let's go.

questions.q: According to the three SCD2 date range invariants named in the lesson, what should be true for any given date D within an entity's version history?
choices: At most one row has EffectiveFrom <= D <= EffectiveTo, and — for dates within the tracked history — exactly one row should cover D with no gap
Every row in the dimension should have the same EffectiveFrom and EffectiveTo values
D should never fall within any version's date range at all
Exactly two rows must always cover any given date to allow for correction records
questions.right: Right — non-overlapping and gapless together mean exactly one row is valid on any given date within the tracked history. Two rows covering the same date is the overlap failure; zero rows covering it is the gap failure.
questions.wrong: The lesson names three invariants: non-overlapping (at most one row covers any date D), gapless (for dates between the first and last version, exactly one row covers D), and current-only (exactly one row is flagged as the current version). Put together, for any date within the tracked history, precisely one row — not zero, not two — should be the valid version for that date. Zero is a gap; two is an overlap; both break point-in-time joins.

questions.q: What does it mean if `LAG(EffectiveTo) OVER (PARTITION BY CustomerID ORDER BY EffectiveFrom)` shows a gap greater than 1 day before the current row's EffectiveFrom?
choices: There's a period of time where no dimension row is valid for that customer — a gap in the SCD2 history
The customer has been deleted from the dimension table entirely
SQL Server will automatically reject the load and roll back the transaction
The customer's IsActive flag has been incorrectly set to 0
questions.right: Right — that's exactly the gap failure mode the lesson describes: a stretch of days with no valid dimension row for that customer, meaning any order falling in that window can't be matched to a customer state at all.
questions.wrong: The lesson explains this directly: a gap exists when the new version's EffectiveFrom starts more than one day after the previous version's EffectiveTo — meaning there's a stretch of calendar time where no dimension row is valid for that customer. Any fact table order that falls within that gap period will fail to join to any customer dimension row, silently excluding it from customer-level analysis, exactly as described in the live scenario's 120 affected customers.

questions.q: What does it mean if `SUM(IsCurrent)` (the count of current-flagged rows) is greater than `COUNT(DISTINCT CustomerID)` in Step 3's summary?
choices: At least one customer has more than one row simultaneously flagged as the current version — the overlap failure at its worst
The dimension table is missing rows for some customers entirely
It indicates a rounding error in the SUM calculation that requires no action
Every customer in the table has exactly two current versions, which is expected behavior
questions.right: Right — if there are more "current" flags than customers, at least one customer has two rows simultaneously claiming to be current. That's the specific failure the lesson calls the worst case of an overlap.
questions.wrong: The lesson states this directly: more current rows than distinct customers means at least one customer has two active versions simultaneously — the ETL created a new current row without properly closing out the old one. Any query filtering on `IsCurrent = 1` for that customer would return both rows, doubling that customer's contribution to any aggregate built on top of the dimension.

G14-T01.close: The three SCD2 invariants, gaps as unmatched date ranges, and multiple-current-rows as the worst overlap case — SCD2 validation covered. Next: Fact Table Grain Validation, checking that every row in a fact table represents the same level of detail.

G14-T02.open: Fact Table Grain Validation — mixing two levels of detail in one fact table (a whole order vs. a single line item) is one of the sneakiest ways to silently inflate a revenue total.

questions.q: What does the fact table's "grain" refer to, according to this lesson?
choices: The lowest level of detail represented by each row — the specific combination of dimension keys that uniquely identifies what one row means
The physical storage size of each row on disk
The number of columns in the fact table
The refresh frequency of the ETL job that loads the table
questions.right: Right — grain is about meaning, not size or schedule. It's the answer to "what does one row of this table represent?"
questions.wrong: The lesson defines grain precisely: it's the lowest level of detail each row represents, defined by the combination of dimension foreign keys that uniquely identifies it — for example, "one row per order-product combination." It has nothing to do with storage size or refresh timing; it's a statement about what a single row means, and mixing two different meanings in one table (order-level rows alongside line-item-level rows) is exactly the failure this technique detects.

questions.q: Why does a NULL in a dimension key column (like ProductID) act as "the hallmark of a mixed-grain fact table", according to the lesson?
choices: It typically means the row can't be assigned to a dimension member at the intended grain level, suggesting some rows carry all keys (fine-grained) while others carry only some (coarser-grained)
NULL values in dimension keys always indicate a hardware failure during the ETL load
SQL Server automatically converts NULL dimension keys to the value -1
A NULL dimension key means the row has been soft-deleted and should be ignored
questions.right: Right — a NULL key is the fingerprint of a row that simply doesn't have all the detail the intended grain requires, which is exactly what happens when a coarser-grained row (like an order header) gets loaded alongside fine-grained ones (order lines).
questions.wrong: The lesson's live scenario makes this concrete: when the intended grain is one-row-per-product, but some rows come from an order-header-level source with no ProductID at all, those rows show NULL in the ProductID column — they simply don't have that level of detail. The lesson calls this the hallmark of mixed grain: some rows have all the keys the intended grain requires, others have only a subset, because they were sourced from two structurally different levels of detail.

questions.q: Why must a degenerate dimension (like OrderID stored directly in the fact table) be non-NULL, according to the lesson?
choices: Without it, the fact row cannot be traced back to its source transaction at all
SQL Server enforces a NOT NULL constraint on all degenerate dimensions automatically
A NULL degenerate dimension would cause the fact table's primary key to be duplicated
Degenerate dimensions are never allowed to contain data of any kind
questions.right: Right — the whole point of a degenerate dimension is traceability back to the source. A NULL there breaks that link entirely, with nothing else in the row to fall back on.
questions.wrong: The lesson explains the purpose of a degenerate dimension directly: it's the source transaction key (OrderID, InvoiceNumber) stored right in the fact table rather than in a separate dimension table, and its entire purpose is letting you trace a fact row back to its origin. A NULL value there defeats that purpose completely — there's no other column standing in as a fallback identifier, so the fact becomes untraceable to its source.

G14-T02.close: Grain as "what one row means," NULL keys as the mixed-grain fingerprint, and degenerate dimensions as the traceability link — grain validation covered. Next: Dimension Key Integrity, checking that fact rows actually point at real dimension members.

G14-T03.open: Dimension Key Integrity in Star Schema — a fact row referencing a dimension key that doesn't exist, or exists but is marked inactive, both quietly exclude revenue from reports without any error being raised.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say LEFT JOIN is more efficient than NOT EXISTS for this particular use case — returning the full row context of failing fact records?
choices: LEFT JOIN naturally returns all the columns from both the fact and dimension side in one pass, which is exactly what's needed when you want to see the failing rows in full detail
NOT EXISTS cannot be combined with a WHERE clause under any circumstances
LEFT JOIN is always faster than NOT EXISTS regardless of what columns are being returned
NOT EXISTS only works when the dimension table has fewer than 100 rows
questions.right: Right — it's about what each one is naturally suited for. LEFT JOIN gives you the row plus all the dimension columns (NULL when unmatched) in a single query, which is exactly the shape needed to review each failing order.
questions.wrong: The lesson frames this as a fit-for-purpose choice, not a universal performance claim: since Step 1 wants to review the full context of each failing order — its OrderID, CustomerID, and every dimension status flag — a LEFT JOIN naturally returns all of those columns from both sides in a single pass. NOT EXISTS is a good fit for a simple existence check, but it doesn't naturally give you extra columns from the table you're checking against.

questions.q: Why is a fact row referencing an inactive dimension member (IsActive = 0) described as "technically valid" but still a concern?
choices: The foreign key itself is valid — the referenced row exists — but many BI tools filter on IsActive = 1 by default, silently excluding these fact rows from reports
SQL Server automatically rejects any INSERT that references an inactive dimension row
IsActive = 0 always means the dimension row's primary key has been physically deleted
It's only a concern for the Customers table, never for the Products table
questions.right: Right — referential integrity and business relevance are two separate questions. The key exists (integrity is fine), but a default active-only filter can silently drop that row from every report anyway.
questions.wrong: The lesson draws this exact distinction: from a pure referential integrity standpoint, the key is valid because the referenced dimension row genuinely exists — it just happens to be marked inactive. The business concern is separate: many BI tools apply an `IsActive = 1` filter by default, which would silently exclude any fact row tied to an inactive dimension member from current reports, even though the underlying data relationship is perfectly intact.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what are the three possible explanations for an unreferenced dimension member (a customer or product with no matching fact rows)?
choices: A legitimate case (registered but never ordered, or catalogued but never sold), or a placeholder/test row that should be excluded from user-facing reports
A SQL Server licensing limitation, a network timeout, and a corrupted index
It always indicates the dimension table needs to be dropped and rebuilt
It can only happen if the fact table has more rows than the dimension table
questions.right: Right — the lesson is careful not to treat every unreferenced row as a problem. Some are perfectly legitimate (a registered-but-inactive customer); others are placeholder or test data that shouldn't be in reports at all.
questions.wrong: The lesson gives these specific possibilities: customers who registered but never placed an order (legitimate), products added to the catalogue but never sold (also legitimate), or placeholder/test dimension rows left over from development that should be filtered out of user-facing reports. It's presented as something worth investigating, not something automatically wrong — the interpretation depends on which of these three explains the specific case.

G14-T03.close: LEFT JOIN as the right tool for full-context review, active-vs-inactive as a separate concern from integrity, and unreferenced members as sometimes-legitimate — dimension key integrity covered. Next: Late-Arriving Facts, when a transaction shows up long after its reporting period has closed.

G14-T04.open: Late-Arriving Facts Detection — a transaction that arrives weeks after its own event date can quietly invalidate a report the board has already seen.

questions.q: What's the difference between a transaction's "event date" and its "load date", as the lesson defines them?
choices: Event date is when the business event actually occurred and determines the reporting period it belongs to; load date is when the record entered the warehouse and determines which load batch included it
Event date and load date are two names for the exact same column, used interchangeably
Event date only applies to Transactions, while load date only applies to Orders
Load date always comes before event date in a correctly functioning system
questions.right: Right — one date is about the business reality (when did this actually happen), the other is about the pipeline (when did the warehouse learn about it). The gap between them is exactly what "lateness" measures.
questions.wrong: The lesson defines these as two genuinely different things: event date (OrderDate) is when the business event actually occurred, and it's what determines which reporting period the revenue belongs to. Load date is when the record entered the data warehouse, determining which nightly batch picked it up. The whole concept of "lateness" is the gap between these two — a transaction that happened in March but wasn't loaded until April is late by that gap, even though both dates are individually accurate.

questions.q: Why does the lesson describe the SCD2 dimension mismatch as a "specific DW integrity problem" caused by late-arriving facts?
choices: The correct dimension version for a late fact is the one effective as of its event date, not its load date, but by the time it arrives the customer's dimension state may have already changed
SCD2 dimensions cannot store more than one version per customer, causing an automatic conflict
Late-arriving facts are always rejected by SCD2 dimension tables and never loaded at all
The problem only affects SCD Type 1 dimensions, never SCD Type 2
questions.right: Right — the correct lookup key for a late fact is its own event date, not "whenever it happened to arrive." Standard ETL tooling that always joins to the current dimension state gets this wrong by default.
questions.wrong: The lesson explains this precisely: a March transaction should be joined to the March version of the customer dimension — the segment or state the customer was in back then. But if that transaction doesn't arrive until April, and the customer's dimension has since changed (a new SCD2 version), a naive ETL join would attach it to the April state instead. The lesson notes this requires a special lookup — as of the event date, not the load date — that most standard ETL tools don't apply by default.

questions.q: Why does the lesson describe the 30-day lateness threshold as "illustrative" rather than a fixed rule?
choices: The appropriate threshold should align with the organisation's actual reporting cadence — weekly reconciliation, month-end close, or quarter-end, each implying a different threshold
30 days is a hard-coded SQL Server system limit that cannot be changed
The threshold only matters for companies with fewer than 100 customers
It's illustrative because DATEDIFF() cannot calculate periods longer than 30 days
questions.right: Right — the threshold should track how often the business actually closes its books, not an arbitrary fixed number. A weekly-reconciliation business needs a much tighter threshold than one that only closes quarterly.
questions.wrong: The lesson gives concrete examples of why the right threshold varies: a 7-day threshold would catch transactions that missed weekly reconciliation, a 45-day threshold would catch ones that missed month-end close, and a 90-day threshold would catch ones that missed quarter-end. The 30-day figure used in the query is just a reasonable illustrative default — the actual threshold should be tuned to match how frequently the specific organisation actually closes its books.

G14-T04.close: Event date vs load date, the SCD2-mismatch trap for late arrivals, and threshold tuning against the real reporting cadence — late-arriving fact detection covered. Next: Aggregate Consistency, checking that summary tables actually agree with the detail they're supposed to summarize.

G14-T05.open: Aggregate Consistency Between Fact Layers — when a dashboard's monthly total doesn't match the sum of its own daily totals, something in the pipeline broke, and this technique finds exactly where.

questions.q: Why does this lesson use FULL OUTER JOIN rather than LEFT JOIN when comparing the two fact layers for consistency?
choices: A LEFT JOIN would miss periods present only in the second table (e.g. Transaction periods with no matching Orders); FULL OUTER JOIN catches gaps in either direction at once
FULL OUTER JOIN executes faster than LEFT JOIN on tables with matching row counts
LEFT JOIN cannot be used together with a CASE expression in the same query
FULL OUTER JOIN automatically deduplicates rows that appear in both tables
questions.right: Right — the same reasoning as elsewhere in this course: a LEFT JOIN only guarantees you catch gaps missing from one specific side. FULL OUTER JOIN is the only join type that surfaces a mismatch regardless of which side it's missing from.
questions.wrong: The lesson explains this the same way orphan/gap detection is explained elsewhere in this course: a LEFT JOIN (from the Orders side) would catch periods missing from Transactions, but would miss the reverse case — periods with Transactions but no matching Orders. Only FULL OUTER JOIN catches both directions of mismatch in a single query, which matters here because either direction represents a real consistency problem worth surfacing.

questions.q: Why does the lesson normalise the variance as a percentage (`ABS(variance) / total × 100`) rather than relying on the raw pound-value difference alone?
choices: The same raw variance means very different things depending on the size of the period total — £100 is immaterial against £100,000 but material against £1,000
SQL Server cannot compare two DECIMAL values directly without first converting one to a percentage
Percentage variance is always a smaller number than the raw pound variance, making reports look better
Raw pound variances can only be calculated for values greater than £1,000
questions.right: Right — scale matters. The same absolute gap is a rounding error in one context and a real red flag in another; normalising by the total is what makes a single fixed threshold meaningful across periods of very different size.
questions.wrong: The lesson makes this exact comparison: a £100 variance on a £100,000 period total is 0.1% — immaterial. The same £100 variance on a £1,000 period total is 10% — clearly material. A raw pound-value threshold would either miss real problems in small periods or flag noise in large ones; normalising by dividing by the total is what lets a single materiality threshold (like 0.1%–1%) apply meaningfully across periods of very different scale.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say a count mismatch and an amount mismatch "have different root causes and different remediation paths"?
choices: A count match with an amount mismatch suggests individual values differ; an amount match with a count mismatch suggests duplicate or split records that happen to net out to the same total
A count mismatch always means the database has run out of storage space
An amount mismatch can only occur if the database's collation setting is misconfigured
Count and amount mismatches are actually the same underlying problem described two different ways
questions.right: Right — these two checks catch genuinely different failure shapes. One is about individual values being wrong; the other is about the wrong number of records existing, even if their sum happens to still add up.
questions.wrong: The lesson distinguishes these directly: if the counts match but the amounts don't, individual transaction values themselves differ between layers — a data or transformation issue. If the amounts match but the counts don't, it points to duplicate or split records whose totals happen to net out to the same figure — a structural, not a value, problem. Because the underlying cause is different in each case, fixing one requires a different investigation than fixing the other, which is why the lesson checks them as two separate signals rather than one combined check.

G14-T05.close: FULL OUTER JOIN for catching mismatches in either direction, percentage variance for scale-independent materiality, and count-vs-amount as two distinct failure signatures — aggregate consistency covered. Next: Incremental Load Completeness, verifying an ETL batch actually brought over everything it was supposed to.

G14-T06.open: Incremental Load Completeness Check — an ETL job can finish successfully, report zero errors, and still have silently dropped a chunk of records. This technique is how you'd actually catch that.

questions.q: Why is OrderID sequence gap detection (`LEAD(OrderID) - OrderID - 1`) described as more precise than a simple count comparison between source and destination?
choices: It identifies exactly which specific IDs are missing, not just how many records are missing in total
Sequence gap detection runs faster than any count-based comparison regardless of table size
Count comparison can only be used on tables with fewer than 1,000 rows
Sequence gap detection eliminates the need to compare source and destination at all
questions.right: Right — a count tells you "how many," a sequence gap tells you exactly "which ones." That precision is what lets someone go straight to the missing records instead of hunting for them.
questions.wrong: The lesson makes this distinction directly: count comparison between source and destination tells you *how many* records are missing overall, but sequence gap detection using LEAD() tells you precisely *which* IDs are missing — the exact range between two consecutive loaded IDs. That precision means the team can go straight to querying the source system for those specific missing IDs, rather than having to reconcile the entire dataset to find them.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say a 3-month rolling average catches failures that a simple count comparison alone cannot?
choices: If the source itself genuinely has fewer records that month (a real business decline), a missing-record failure and an honest low-volume month look identical from count comparison alone — the rolling average gives a sense of what's actually "normal" to compare against
Count comparison cannot be computed for any month with fewer than 100 orders
A rolling average is required by SQL Server syntax whenever GROUP BY is used with COUNT(*)
The rolling average always produces a higher number than simple count comparison
questions.right: Right — this is exactly the blind spot: if the source and destination counts agree but both are honestly low due to a slow business month, count comparison alone sees nothing wrong. The rolling average adds a sense of what's actually normal, so an unusual drop stands out on its own.
questions.wrong: The lesson names this exact edge case: if the source system itself has fewer records for a given month — a genuine business slowdown — then source-to-destination count comparison shows perfect agreement, because both sides are honestly low. That looks identical to a correctly-loaded low-volume month. The rolling average adds context count comparison alone doesn't have: it tells you whether this month's volume, compared to the recent trend, looks unusually low regardless of whether the source and destination currently agree.

questions.q: Why does the lesson describe over-loads (destination count greater than source count) as "often harder to detect than under-loads"?
choices: An inflated total looks like business growth, so it doesn't trigger the same suspicion an unexpectedly low total naturally would
SQL Server does not provide any built-in function capable of detecting duplicate records
Over-loads can only occur once per calendar year, making them statistically rare
Under-loads always produce a SQL Server error message, while over-loads never do
questions.right: Right — a bigger-than-expected number doesn't look broken on the surface. It takes an explicit destination-vs-source comparison to reveal that the extra records shouldn't be there at all.
questions.wrong: The lesson makes this point directly: an under-load produces a total that's obviously too low, which tends to draw attention on its own. An over-load, by contrast, produces a total that's too high — which superficially looks like the business is simply doing better than expected, rather than looking broken. Without an explicit comparison against the source count, inflated numbers from duplicate loads can go unnoticed precisely because they don't look like a problem.

G14-T06.close: Sequence gaps for pinpoint precision, rolling averages for context count comparison alone lacks, and over-loads hiding behind apparent growth — incremental load completeness covered. Next: SCD Type 1 Override Audit, recovering some visibility into history that overwrite-in-place destroys.

G14-T07.open: Slowly Changing Dimension Type 1 Override Audit — SCD1 overwrites history by design, which is fine until someone asks a question the design made unanswerable.

questions.q: Why does the lesson describe a change-log table as "the missing intermediate between pure SCD1 and SCD2"?
choices: SCD1 keeps no history at all, and SCD2 keeps full history as new dimension rows; a change log sits between them by overwriting the dimension like SCD1 does, while still recording what changed and when in a separate table
A change-log table is simply another name for an SCD2 dimension table
SCD1 and SCD2 are identical in every respect except for their table names
A change-log table replaces the need for a dimension table entirely
questions.right: Right — it gets you a documented trail of changes without taking on the full complexity (and query-time effective-date filtering) that comes with SCD2.
questions.wrong: The lesson frames these as a spectrum: pure SCD1 overwrites in place and keeps no history whatsoever; SCD2 preserves full history by inserting new dated rows for every change. A change-log table is a middle ground — the dimension itself still gets overwritten SCD1-style (simple to query, no effective-date filtering needed), but every overwrite is separately recorded in a log table capturing the old value, the new value, and when the change happened. It gets you an audit trail without taking on SCD2's full complexity.

questions.q: Why does the change-detection logic use `ISNULL(c.Country, '') <> ISNULL(b.Country, '')` instead of comparing `c.Country <> b.Country` directly?
choices: NULL <> NULL evaluates to unknown (neither true nor false) in SQL, so a direct comparison would fail to correctly identify an unchanged NULL-to-NULL value as "no change"
SQL Server does not allow the <> operator to be used on VARCHAR columns under any circumstances
ISNULL() is required by SQL Server syntax whenever two columns are compared in a WHERE or CASE clause
The ISNULL wrapper converts both columns to a numeric type before comparison
questions.right: Right — SQL's three-valued logic is the trap here. NULL compared to NULL isn't TRUE and isn't FALSE, it's UNKNOWN, and a CASE expression treats UNKNOWN as "didn't match" — which would misclassify a genuinely unchanged NULL as changed.
questions.wrong: The lesson explains this precisely: in SQL's three-valued logic, `NULL <> NULL` evaluates to UNKNOWN, not TRUE or FALSE. A CASE expression checking that condition would fail to correctly treat a NULL-to-NULL transition (genuinely unchanged) as "unchanged" — it needs to explicitly be TRUE or FALSE to route correctly. Wrapping both sides in ISNULL() converts NULL to a comparable placeholder value first, so two NULLs compare as equal (via the placeholder) and the comparison behaves as a real change check.

questions.q: Why does the lesson call the retroactive effect of an SCD1 attribute change "correct for some use cases but wrong for historical analysis"?
choices: Under SCD1, all historical fact rows for that entity now show the new attribute value applied retroactively — accurate for "who is this customer right now" but wrong for "what was true about them when this specific order happened"
SCD1 changes are only ever applied to numeric columns, never to text columns like Country
Historical analysis is technically impossible in any data warehouse regardless of SCD strategy
The retroactive effect only occurs when the customer's IsActive flag changes from 1 to 0
questions.right: Right — that's the fundamental trade-off SCD1 makes. It's genuinely correct for "what's true about this customer today," and genuinely wrong for "what was true about them back when this order happened."
questions.wrong: The lesson's own example makes this concrete: a customer who changed from "UK" to "Germany" in July will, under SCD1, now appear as a German customer for every order they placed from January through June too — even though they were genuinely a UK customer at the time those orders happened. That retroactive view is exactly right for current-state analysis (who is this customer today?) but exactly wrong for historical analysis (what segment was this customer in when this specific order was placed?) — SCD1 can only give you one of those two answers, never both.

G14-T07.close: Change logs as a middle ground between SCD1 and SCD2, ISNULL as the fix for SQL's NULL-comparison trap, and the retroactive-correctness trade-off — SCD1 audit covered. Next: Data Lineage and Source Traceability, tracing a number on a report all the way back to its source record.

G14-T08.open: Data Lineage and Source Traceability — when an auditor asks which exact source records a reported figure came from, "we transformed it somewhere in the pipeline" is not an acceptable answer.

questions.q: What three components does the lesson say are required for complete data lineage on a warehouse record?
choices: Which source system it came from, its unique identifier in that source system, and which ETL load batch brought it into the warehouse
Its row count, column count, and total storage size
Its creation date, its last-modified date, and its owner's username
Its primary key, its foreign keys, and its check constraints
questions.right: Right — source system, source record ID, and load batch ID together. With all three, any warehouse row can be traced back to the exact source row and the exact moment it was loaded.
questions.wrong: The lesson names these three specifically: which source system the record originated from (SourceSystemID), its unique identifier within that source system (SourceRecordID), and which ETL load batch actually brought it into the warehouse (LoadBatchID / CorrelationID). Together, these let any record in the warehouse be traced back to the exact source row and the exact time it was loaded — which is precisely what the compliance officer in the live scenario needed and couldn't get without them.

questions.q: Why does the lesson distinguish "duplicate lineage" (same SourceRecordID loaded twice) from an application-layer duplicate (the same business event recorded twice)?
choices: In duplicate lineage, the business event genuinely happened once but the ETL process loaded it into the warehouse twice; the business layer itself is not at fault
Duplicate lineage can only happen to records loaded on a Friday
They are actually the same failure, just described using different terminology
Application-layer duplicates are always more severe than duplicate lineage issues
questions.right: Right — the underlying business event is fine; it happened exactly once. The problem is entirely on the loading side, which also means the fix is entirely on the loading side (dedupe the ETL), not a source-system correction.
questions.wrong: The lesson draws this line specifically: duplicate lineage means the source record itself is genuinely singular — the business event happened exactly once — but something in the ETL process (a re-run watermark reset, a retry after partial failure, a combined full-plus-incremental load) caused it to be loaded into the warehouse more than once. That's a pipeline defect, not a business-layer error, which matters because the fix is entirely on the loading side rather than requiring any correction to the source system.

questions.q: Why does the lesson treat an amount discrepancy between an order and its linked transaction as worth investigating, rather than dismissing it as normal rounding?
choices: It could indicate an undocumented transformation was applied during ETL — currency conversion, tax addition, or discount application — that changed the amount without being recorded or verified
Amount discrepancies are always caused by a corrupted TransactionID column
SQL Server automatically rounds all DECIMAL values to the nearest whole number during a JOIN
An amount discrepancy always means the customer cancelled their order after payment
questions.right: Right — the concern isn't the discrepancy itself, it's what it might be hiding: a transformation nobody documented or reviewed against business rules, quietly changing figures between the source and the warehouse.
questions.wrong: The lesson frames the concern specifically around undocumented transformation: if the order amount and the linked transaction amount genuinely differ by more than a rounding tolerance, something changed the value somewhere in the pipeline — currency conversion, tax being added, a discount being applied — and that transformation may never have been documented or reviewed against actual business rules. The lineage audit's job is to surface these discrepancies so someone can verify whether the transformation was intentional and correct, not to assume it's benign rounding.

G14-T08.close: The three-part lineage requirement, duplicate lineage as an ETL-side (not business-side) failure, and amount discrepancies as undocumented-transformation flags — data lineage covered. Last one in this group: Bridge Table and Many-to-Many Relationship Integrity.

G14-T09.open: Last one in DW/SCD Specific — Bridge Table and Many-to-Many Relationship Integrity. A join that silently multiplies rows is one of the most financially dangerous mistakes in a data warehouse, because the query still runs and returns a number that looks completely plausible.

questions.q: Why does joining Orders to Transactions without aggregation inflate the total revenue figure, according to the lesson's own worked example?
choices: When an order matches more than one transaction row, that order's row is replicated once per matching transaction, and any SUM computed afterward counts the order's amount multiple times
SQL Server automatically doubles every DECIMAL value during a JOIN operation
The Transactions table contains a corrupted Amount column with incorrect values
TotalAmount and Amount refer to two completely unrelated business concepts that should never be summed together
questions.right: Right — that's exactly the mechanism the lesson's own numbers demonstrate: 20 orders become 27 rows after the join because some orders match more than one transaction, and summing over those 27 rows overcounts the orders that got replicated.
questions.wrong: The lesson's Step 5 makes this concrete with real numbers: 20 orders, when joined to Transactions without first aggregating, produce 27 rows — because some orders match more than one transaction row, and each match replicates that order's row. Summing TotalAmount over those 27 replicated rows counts the multiplied orders' amounts more than once, inflating the total from £27,610 to £37,274 purely from the join structure, with no change to the underlying data.

questions.q: What does it mean if a bridge table's weighting factors for one entity sum to 1.5 instead of 1.0?
choices: Any total computed by applying those weights to that entity will be systematically overstated by 50%
The bridge table will automatically reject any new associations until the weights are corrected
It indicates the entity has been assigned to exactly 1.5 categories, which is a valid business state
SQL Server will round the weights down to 1.0 automatically during aggregation
questions.right: Right — weights are supposed to represent a fair 1/N split, and if they sum above 1.0, whatever total gets computed from them will be inflated by exactly that excess, in this case 50%.
questions.wrong: The lesson states this directly: weights are meant to sum to 1.0 per entity so that a weighted total represents a correct, single-counted figure. If they instead sum to 1.5, any total computed by applying those weights (`SUM(Amount) x Weight`) will be systematically overstated by 50% — the exact scale of the error is proportional to how far the weight sum exceeds 1.0, which is why the lesson's live scenario ties incorrect weighting directly to inflated campaign ROI figures.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend "aggregate-first" as the canonical remedy for fan-out risk?
choices: Computing the summary at the fact table's own grain before joining ensures each fact row's total is already correct, so the subsequent join can't multiply it regardless of how many matching rows exist on the other side
Aggregate-first is required by SQL Server syntax whenever a JOIN clause is used with SUM()
It eliminates the need for a bridge table or weighting factors of any kind
It only works when the fact table has fewer than 50 rows
questions.right: Right — aggregate first, then join. Once each order's transactions are already summed into one row, joining to that pre-aggregated result can't multiply anything, no matter how many transaction rows originally existed for that order.
questions.wrong: The lesson explains the mechanism: computing `SUM(t.Amount)` per OrderID in a CTE first, then joining that already-aggregated result to Orders, guarantees one row per order going into the join — regardless of how many transaction rows existed for that order before aggregation. Since the multiplication only happens when a JOIN encounters multiple matching rows on one side, removing that multiplicity before the join (by aggregating first) removes the fan-out risk entirely, rather than trying to correct for it after the fact.

G14-T09.close: Fan-out as row replication through a JOIN, weight-sum errors as proportional overstatement, and aggregate-first as the structural fix — that closes out DW/SCD Specific, and G12-G14 of this pre-authorized programme. Nine techniques in this group: SCD2 gaps/overlaps, fact grain, dimension key integrity, late-arriving facts, aggregate consistency, incremental load completeness, SCD1 audit, data lineage, and bridge table integrity.

G15-T01.open: Welcome to ETL/Load Process — you've opened Staging Table Row Count Reconciliation, checking that records survive every stage of the pipeline instead of quietly vanishing along the way. Three questions.

questions.q: In the stage-count waterfall, what does the lesson say distinguishes an "expected" record drop from an "unexpected" one?
choices: Loss at a filter stage (a business rule excluding records on purpose) is expected; loss at a JOIN stage (which should find a match for every record) is unexpected unless referential integrity is broken
Any drop greater than 10 records is automatically unexpected, regardless of which stage it happens at
All record loss during ETL is expected and never needs individual investigation
Loss is only unexpected if it happens on the very first stage of the pipeline
questions.right: Right — a filter is supposed to drop records; a JOIN is supposed to match every one. That's exactly the distinction the lesson draws: expected loss has a business rule behind it, unexpected loss means something's broken.
questions.wrong: The lesson draws this line specifically: dropping records at a filter stage (like keeping only Delivered orders) is expected — that's the business rule doing its job. Dropping records at a JOIN stage is a different story: a JOIN should find a match for every record unless referential integrity is genuinely broken, so unexplained loss there points to real orphaned data, not an intended filter.

questions.q: What does it mean if a stage in the waterfall shows MORE records than the prior stage, according to the lesson?
choices: A fan-out has occurred — one record joined to multiple rows in another table, replicating the original record
SQL Server automatically doubles row counts whenever a UNION ALL is used
It always means the ETL pipeline completed successfully with no issues
It indicates the source system added new records during the ETL run
questions.right: Right — a stage growing instead of shrinking is the fan-out signature: something on the other side of a join matched more than once, replicating rows rather than filtering them.
questions.wrong: The lesson names this directly: a record GAIN at any stage signals a fan-out — one record on one side of a JOIN matched multiple rows on the other side, replicating that original record rather than passing it through untouched. It's flagged as the specific trigger to investigate JOIN cardinality and consider adding a GROUP BY or deduplication step.

questions.q: Why does the lesson describe the DECLARE-and-compare pattern in Step 4 as "the simplest form of control total verification"?
choices: It stores the source and destination counts as variables and does one direct arithmetic comparison — if the variance isn't zero, the load is flagged as incomplete without needing to inspect individual records
DECLARE statements automatically fix any row count mismatch they detect
It requires scanning every individual row in both tables one at a time
It can only be used when the source and destination tables have identical column structures
questions.right: Right — it's a single subtraction between two stored totals. No row-by-row inspection needed to know whether something's off; the variance alone tells you whether to keep digging.
questions.wrong: The lesson calls this the simplest form specifically because it just captures @SourceCount and @DestCount as two variables and computes @Variance = @SourceCount - @DestCount — one arithmetic comparison, no row-level inspection required. If @Variance isn't 0, that's the signal the load hasn't transferred the expected number of records and the reason needs investigating before the load is accepted as complete.

G15-T01.close: Expected filter loss vs unexpected JOIN loss, record gain as the fan-out signal, and control totals as the simplest completeness check — staging reconciliation covered. Next: Transformation Rule Validation, checking that business rules were actually applied, not just executed.

G15-T02.open: Transformation Rule Validation — an ETL job can complete with zero errors while still getting every phone number, country code, or email format subtly wrong. This technique catches that.

questions.q: Why does the lesson compute an `ExpectedNormalisedPhone` column showing what a phone number *should* look like after transformation?
choices: It serves two purposes: confirming the transformation logic is correct before applying it at scale, and producing a preview of the correction that could be used to fix already-loaded records
SQL Server requires every transformation check to include a preview column by default
It replaces the need to check the actual Phone column entirely
It only works for phone numbers with international dialling codes
questions.right: Right — a dual-purpose column. It validates the transformation logic itself, and it doubles as a ready-made correction script for records that never got transformed.
questions.wrong: The lesson names two purposes directly: first, it confirms the transformation logic itself is correct before it's applied at scale — you can see what the fix would produce. Second, it effectively produces a correction preview: the value that an UPDATE statement would need to write to apply the missing transformation to records that were loaded without it.

questions.q: Why does the lesson describe the VAT rate check (`VATRate NOT IN (0, 5, 20)`) as revealing a possible mapping table problem?
choices: A rate outside the UK's standard rates (like the old 17.5% pre-2011 rate, or a non-UK 25% rate) suggests a mapping table that wasn't updated, or a record from an overseas source that skipped country-specific rate conversion
SQL Server automatically converts all VAT rates to 20% during any numeric transformation
The check only applies to products priced under £10
VATRate can only ever be exactly 0, 5, or 20 in any valid UK dataset by database constraint
questions.right: Right — the specific values named matter: 17.5% is a real historical UK rate (pre-2011), and a rate like 25% points to a non-UK source. Either points at the mapping logic, not a random glitch.
questions.wrong: The lesson gives specific examples: a rate of 17.5% is the old UK standard rate before 2011 — a strong sign the mapping table is stale and wasn't updated to current rates. A rate of 25% isn't a valid UK rate at all, suggesting a record from an overseas source that passed through without the country-specific rate conversion being applied. Both point to a mapping table or transformation gap, not a one-off data entry error.

questions.q: What does the transformation rule summary in Step 6 (Passed/Failed/Nulls/Total per rule) let an analyst do that checking a single record cannot?
choices: It gives a pass/fail scorecard across the whole dataset, showing what fraction of records genuinely conform to each rule — a 58% pass rate flags that a rule needs its logic extended, not just that one record is wrong
It automatically corrects every failing record without further action
It only works if every single record in the table has already passed all rules
It replaces the need for the individual per-record transformation checks entirely
questions.right: Right — one record tells you about one record. The summary tells you whether the transformation rule itself is actually working across the board, which is the real question an ETL owner needs answered.
questions.wrong: The lesson explains the summary's purpose directly: a 100% pass rate confirms a rule is genuinely working across the dataset, while a lower rate — the lesson's own example shows 58% — flags that a meaningful fraction of records still need the rule applied, or that the rule's logic needs to be extended to cover more format variants it currently misses. That's a dataset-wide health signal a single-record check can't give you.

G15-T02.close: The correction-preview pattern, VAT rate as a mapping-table tell, and pass-rate scorecards over single-record checks — transformation rule validation covered. Next: Duplicate Detection During Load, catching records before they're loaded twice.

G15-T03.open: Duplicate Detection During Load — a corrected re-send of yesterday's file, loaded without deduplication, can quietly overstate a week's revenue by hundreds of thousands.

questions.q: Why does the lesson treat exact key duplicates (same OrderID more than once), business-key duplicates (same CustomerID+ProductID+date), and near-duplicates (same customer+amount within days) as needing different detection strategies?
choices: Exact key duplicates are definitively wrong, business-key duplicates may be legitimate or erroneous depending on context, and near-duplicates are probabilistic and require business context to confirm — three different confidence levels needing three different checks
SQL Server only supports one type of duplicate detection query per table
Near-duplicates are always more severe than exact key duplicates
All three types are actually the same underlying problem, just checked with different syntax for convenience
questions.right: Right — three genuinely different confidence levels. An exact key duplicate is unambiguous; a business-key match could be two real same-day orders; a near-duplicate is just a hint that needs a human to confirm.
questions.wrong: The lesson is explicit about the distinction: exact key duplicates (same OrderID) are definitively wrong, since a primary key should prevent them entirely. Business key duplicates might be legitimate (a customer genuinely placing two separate same-day orders) or erroneous (a retry load) — the lesson notes amounts help distinguish which. Near-duplicates are the weakest signal — probabilistic, requiring actual business context to confirm whether they represent a real resubmission or just coincidence.

questions.q: In Step 5's deduplication preview, why does `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY business_key ORDER BY OrderID)` keep the row with rank 1 — the earliest OrderID — as the canonical record?
choices: The earliest-assigned ID is often the correct choice, since it typically represents the first, original occurrence of that record rather than a later duplicate load
SQL Server always requires ORDER BY OrderID specifically inside a PARTITION BY clause
ROW_NUMBER() can only be computed in ascending order, never descending
The earliest OrderID is chosen at random and has no particular significance
questions.right: Right — first occurrence, first ID, generally the canonical original. It's a reasonable default rule for "which copy do we keep" when duplicates are being resolved.
questions.wrong: The lesson frames this as a deliberate default choice, not an arbitrary one: the earliest-assigned ID is often the correct record to keep because it typically represents the first, original occurrence of that business event — later duplicates, by contrast, usually come from a retry, a re-send, or a duplicate load. `WHERE Rn = 1` in a load statement is what actually applies this rule to only bring in the deduplicated set.

questions.q: Why does the lesson call SQL-based deduplication "a compensating control" rather than the primary defence against duplicates?
choices: It detects duplicates that have already gotten in; the real primary controls should be upstream — unique constraints, idempotent ETL design, and source-system deduplication before extraction
SQL deduplication queries are always too slow to run in production environments
Compensating controls are a stronger defence than any upstream constraint could ever be
SQL-based deduplication can only be used once per calendar month due to performance limits
questions.right: Right — it's a safety net, not the main line of defence. The real fix is upstream: prevent duplicates from being created or loaded in the first place, and let the SQL check catch whatever slips through anyway.
questions.wrong: The lesson is explicit about the hierarchy here: the primary control against duplicates should be upstream — unique constraints on the target table, an idempotent ETL design (so re-running the same load twice produces the same result, not double the data), and deduplication at the source system before extraction even happens. SQL-based detection like this technique provides a safety net for when those upstream controls fail, not a substitute for having them in the first place.

G15-T03.close: Three duplicate types needing three confidence levels, earliest-ID as the canonical record, and detection as a safety net rather than the primary defence — duplicate detection covered. Next: Type Coercion and Implicit Conversion Audit, catching values that convert without error but arrive wrong.

G15-T04.open: Type Coercion and Implicit Conversion Audit — TRY_CAST is a deliberately forgiving function, and that forgiveness is exactly what makes silently failed conversions so dangerous.

questions.q: Why does the lesson call TRY_CAST's behaviour "deliberate" even though it can hide failed conversions?
choices: Returning NULL instead of raising an error lets ETL pipelines keep processing without crashing on a single bad value — the tradeoff is that failed conversions become invisible unless the NULL rate is actively monitored
TRY_CAST is a bug in SQL Server that Microsoft has not yet fixed
TRY_CAST always throws a visible warning message, so nothing is actually hidden
TRY_CAST only fails silently when used inside a stored procedure, never in a plain query
questions.right: Right — it's a genuine design tradeoff, not an oversight. The forgiveness that keeps a pipeline running is the exact same behavior that hides a failed conversion unless someone is specifically watching for it.
questions.wrong: The lesson explains this as a real design tradeoff, not a flaw: TRY_CAST returning NULL rather than raising an error means an ETL pipeline can keep processing the rest of a batch without crashing over one malformed value. The cost of that resilience is that failed conversions become invisible by default — comparing the pre-load and post-load NULL rate is what's needed to actually surface where conversion silently failed.

questions.q: Why is a high proportion of round numbers (`TotalAmount = FLOOR(TotalAmount)`) in a financial amount column treated as a possible red flag?
choices: It may indicate precision was lost during a FLOAT-to-DECIMAL conversion, or that the source stores integer cents/pence values that should have been divided by 100 but weren't
Round numbers in financial data are always fabricated or fraudulent
SQL Server cannot store decimal values below £1.00 under any circumstances
It means the currency column was accidentally deleted during transformation
questions.right: Right — two concrete, plausible causes named by the lesson: a lossy FLOAT conversion, or a units mistake where pence/cents values never got divided down to pounds/dollars.
questions.wrong: The lesson names two specific causes: after a FLOAT-to-DECIMAL conversion, values that should have fractional cents often collapse to round integers, indicating lost precision. Separately, some source systems store amounts as integer cents or pence (so £1,499.99 is stored as 149999) — if the ETL forgot to divide by 100, every value would appear as an implausibly large round number. Either way, a high proportion of round numbers is worth investigating rather than assuming it's a coincidence.

questions.q: Why does the lesson describe the DiscountPercent mix-up (0.15 vs 15) as "entirely semantic" rather than a conversion failure?
choices: Both 0.15 and 15 are individually valid numbers that convert without any error — the value that gets loaded is technically correct as a number, but its business meaning (a 0.15% discount vs a 15% discount) is wrong by a factor of 100
SQL Server refuses to store the value 0.15 in any DECIMAL column
